title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 review: More personal than ever before
snippet: The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are all about what’s happening underneath. Headlined by a new Health Sensing System, they bring some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. I’ve spent the last week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s everything you need to know. Buy Apple Watch Series 12 from $390 (Reg. $399) Buy Apple Watch Ultra 4 Black from $780 (Reg. $799) more…
fullText:
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are all about what’s happening underneath. Headlined by a new Health Sensing System, they bring some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years.

I’ve spent the last week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s everything you need to know.

Buy Apple Watch Series 12 from $390 (Reg. $399)

Buy Apple Watch Ultra 4 Black from $780 (Reg. $799)

Design

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 look the same as their predecessors. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in the same two titanium finishes as before: Natural and Black. My review unit is the Natural finish.

For the Apple Watch Series 12, the real design story is in the colors and finishes.

First, there are some very minor changes in the dimensions of the Apple Watch Series 12. Apple’s tech specs page details that the display area is about 2% smaller than the Series 10 and Series 11. The overall pixel count, however, hasn’t changed. With that slight reduction in display area, the casing is about 1mm wider on the Apple Watch Series 12.

In practice, none of this is noticeable in the real world. The Apple Watch’s display still stretches near the edge of the casing. When you think about the revamped health sensing system (more on that below), it’s especially impressive Apple has maintained that design.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is available in three materials: aluminum, titanium, and ceramic.

Aluminum comes in four finishes: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black, and Space Gray. The aluminum version also switches from Ion-X to Ceramic Shield 2 for the front glass.

My Apple Watch Series 12 review unit is the black aluminum finish. Unlike last year’s Jet Black aluminum case, the black Apple Watch Series 12 is a matte finish. I think I’m partial to the Jet Black look personally, but I understand Apple switches things up on a year-to-year basis and it could return at some point in the future.

Space Gray
Light Gold
Dark Bronze

In my hands-on time with all the Apple Watch Series 12 aluminum colors last week, Dark Bronze stood out most. It’s an elegant finish that is unlike any previous aluminum Apple Watch. The Light Gold is also a really nice color for fans of gold. The Apple Watch Series 12 isn’t available in silver aluminum, but the space gray is light enough that I think it will tick that box for most people.

Titanium in Radiant Gold

The Apple Watch Series 12 in titanium is available in two finishes: Radiant Gold and Natural. In comparison, the titanium Apple Watch Series 11 came in Natural, Gold, and Slate.

The Radiant Gold is striking. Based on the appearance and how it differs from last year’s color, I think Apple’s goal is clear: to make the titanium Apple Watch Series 12 look as much like real gold as possible, but without actually using real gold. People have a lot of strong opinions about what “real gold” actually looks like, but to my eye Apple has done a great job with the Radiant Gold titanium on the Series 12.

Pearl white ceramic

Saving the best for last, the Apple Watch Series 12 in ceramic is available in two finishes: Night Blue and Pearl White. The last time Apple released a ceramic watch was with the Series 5 in 2019, and it quickly became a fan favorite.

I only spent a few minutes with the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 at last week’s Apple event. The Night Blue is nice, but I immediately gravitated towards the Pearl White. It’s not quite as white as the Series 5, with a very soft off-white glow to it depending on the lighting.

Health tracking

The big change to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the new Health Sensing System, which brings what I think is the biggest upgrade to the Apple Watch’s health suite in years.

This starts with a new design for sensing hardware. Apple outlines three aspects to this:

Electrodes get more contact area without the sensor growing. This enables better skin contact during ECG readings.

The photodiodes have been redesigned and are now arranged in a ring to capture more reflected light.

The green LEDs are larger, for more reliable readings while you’re moving, and more power efficient.

This enables the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 to take more accurate and more frequent background heart rate measurements. That is, more heart rate readings when not doing a workout.

Previous Apple Watch models attempted to capture your background heart rate every five minutes when you were mostly stationary.

Apple says the new Health Sensing System delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In a study of more than 1,000 participants, Apple says the Series 12 achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer a big improvement. They will capture your heart rate every five seconds, regardless of whether you’re moving or stationary. Having such frequent and accurate heart rate readings unlocks new levels of data and insight.

When measuring your heart rate once every five minutes while stationary, previous Apple Watch models had an inherent blind spot. They either didn’t capture moments where your heart rate increased while not working out, or they captured one or two arbitrary readings somewhere in the middle of those moments.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 not only take more readings, they take readings while you’re in motion. You can see how things like hauling groceries, doing yard work, and shoveling snow impact your heart rate.

Apple has also added several new ways to view your heart rate data. First, the Heart Rate app on Apple Watch has been redesigned, so you can now see your heart rate and a graph of readings from the last two minutes.

There are also two new heart rate complications for your watch face that show your heart rate at a glance.

In my one week with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, I’ve found that added data very insightful. I’m learning more about how little things I do throughout the day impact my heart rate. For example, I can visualize the impact of a late afternoon cup of coffee, or the impact of a stressful moment at work.

Beyond simply giving you more raw data, Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 proactively use the more frequent heart rate readings to enable new features and improvements.

First, Apple says the data enables improved calorie estimates. I haven’t noticed much change in my data here, but it might become clearer once I’ve worn the new Apple Watch for more than a week.

One thing I had hoped to see was the more frequent heart rate measurements would improve automatic workout detection. At least in my testing so far, that doesn’t seem to be the case. 

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 also now sample heart rate variability (HRV) at a higher rate than before. Previously, it captured HRV once every two hours, but the new Apple Watch models enable measurements as often as once every five minutes while at rest.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 also now track recovery HRV, which is best at recognizing daily signals of stress and fatigue. The new Apple Watch models also continue to measure overall HRV, best at identifying broader health signals, as they have done for years.

Furthermore, Apple is integrating recovery HRV measurements into overnight vitals.

Vitals

Speaking of Vitals, Apple is making several changes to the broader Vitals experience with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. First, there’s a new daytime view for Vitals.

Previously, Vitals was an overnight-only report that you would see in the morning. The daytime view shows you your daytime heart rate and HRV, with the idea being you can see if something is out of whack without waiting for your overnight vitals report.

Vitals also now shows you four different categories for your metrics: notably off, slightly off, typical, or favorable. This gives you more granularity than the old two-tier system, which just categorized your metrics as typical or outlier.

I’m a big fan of the Vitals app on Apple Watch, and I’m glad to see Apple making meaningful improvements with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It has routinely caught signs of a looming sickness before I actually felt anything.

The new daytime view will require some additional testing to know just how useful it is, given that it’s limited to just two metrics. Still, there are some really nice improvements to Vitals that tap into the more frequent heart rate and HRV measurements enabled by the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Readiness

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer a new readiness score that aims to distill all of the data your Apple Watch has on you into a single score.

Apple says that readiness factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score. Your readiness score also updates throughout the day based on naps, activity, and daytime heart rate, so it’s dynamic based on new data that comes in.

You can view your readiness score in the Readiness app on Apple Watch, as well as in the Fitness app on iPhone. It’s also available in the redesigned version of the Health app, which is currently available in beta testing.

The biggest Apple Watch competitors have offered similar scores for years, including Whoop (Whoop Recovery) and Oura (Readiness Score). Apple’s addition of its own readiness feature for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is its most direct response yet to those other wearables.

I’ve worn an Oura Ring for the past year, primarily for its Readiness Score. I appreciate that number distilling multiple different metrics into a single number I can glance at each morning. It’s felt like a huge gap in the Apple Watch’s software experience, and I’m glad Apple is taking a similar approach now.

Apple Watch’s Readiness score requires one week of sleep data, and I’ve only had my review units for a week. This means I’ve only gotten one Readiness score thus far, so it’s too early to make a determination on how useful Apple’s version of the feature is.

I’m optimistic given the type of data Apple is taking into account for readiness. I also think Apple is making the right call by using a 0-10 scale, unlike Oura’s 0-100 scale. Here are Apple’s readiness ranges:

0-1: Recover

2-4: Pace Yourself

5-7: Ready

8-10: Go For It

These strike me as straightforward enough, and potentially more actionable than the scores and patronizing (or passive aggressive) recommendations offered by Oura. I look forward to testing it more and comparing the scores directly to Oura in the coming weeks.

For comparison, on a day where my Apple Watch’s readiness score was an 8/10, my Oura Ring’s was an 85/100. 

I also like how Readiness shows which factor pushed your number up or down, whether that’s sleep, activity, or your overnight vitals, and you can tap through to that app for the details.

Performance

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 are both powered by Apple’s new S11 chip, which the company describes as its “most powerful wearable chip.”

This is the first meaningfully new chip for the Apple Watch since the S9 debuted in the Apple Watch Series 9 in 2023. The Apple Watch Series 10’s S10 chip was the same design in a thinner package, and last year’s models didn’t get a new chip at all.

Apple touts that the new S11 chip includes CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine components derived from the A20 Pro chip used in the iPhone 18 Pro. It also reportedly doubles the Apple Watch’s RAM from 2GB to 4GB.

There’s another aspect to the S11 chip: a new always-on processor that can handle complex workloads without tapping into the main chip. Inside it is a secure exclave, a hardware-isolated compartment to keep microphone data for Audio Intelligence private and secure.

In practice, Apple says the S11 chip, combined with the always-on processor, plays a role in multiple Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 features:

It works in conjunction with the new Health Sensing System to provide the higher-frequency heart rate readings.

It helps power the Audio Intelligence features like Siri Recap (more on that below).

It runs the redesigned pedometer model that Apple says is more accurate, including when your arms are stationary (like pushing a stroller).

In comparison to my Apple Watch Ultra 3, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 feel quicker when launching new apps, scrolling through menus, and doing basic interactions with Siri AI. To me, however, it shines by playing such a vital role in powering the aforementioned new health features.

Battery life

The Apple Watch Series 12 features a slightly larger battery, combined with the improved power efficiency of the Health Sensing System and S11 chip. Here are Apple’s battery claims for Apple Watch Series 12:

24 hrs normal use (unchanged from Series 11)

38 hrs Low Power Mode (unchanged from Series 11)

10 hrs outdoor workout, up 2 hrs

Apple also touts faster charging in select scenarios:

Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking with a 5-minute fast charge

Up to 12 hours of battery life with a 15-minute fast charge

Up to 80 percent battery charge in about 30 minutes (unchanged)

Those top two line items stood out to me in my testing of the Apple Watch Series 12. With Apple Watch’s increasing focus on sleep tracking, having a way to quickly top up before bed is very important.

For Apple Watch Ultra 4, which also has a larger battery, Apple says:

50 hours normal use, up from 42 on Ultra 3

84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 on Ultra 3

Workouts: 18 hours standard (up from 14), 25 hrs Extended (up from 20), and 45 hours Max Extended

Up to 18 hours of battery life with a 15-min fast charge, up from 12 hours on Ultra 3

In my testing, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lives up to Apple’s battery life claims. In my real-world test, I charged it to 100% around 8 p.m. on Sunday and didn’t put it back on the charger until 8 p.m. on Tuesday. That’s 48 hours on a single charge, including 90 minutes of workout tracking, three hours away from my iPhone, and two nights of sleep tracking.

Odds and ends

There’s a new Steps complication for your watch face that updates your step count in real-time. I love it.

Apple has redesigned the Ocean Band for the Apple Watch Ultra. It’s now made from a translucent silicone material and comes in translucent gray, translucent kelp, and translucent black. In addition to the different appearance, the new Ocean Band style also feels lighter on my wrist.

There’s a new Siri Modular watch face, which is also backwards compatible. Zac covered it in detail here.

More to come

This is really only the start of what to expect from Apple Watch this year.

First, Apple is working on a completely redesigned version of the Health app, with a new Longevity tab and metrics like Health Age. I’m eager to try the new Health app. Apple says it’s coming in a software update later this year, and it’s available in beta as of Wednesday afternoon.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will also add new Audio Intelligence features later this year, including Live Rewind and Siri Recap. 

Live Rewind lets you recall what was just said in the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet by double-pressing the Digital Crown. Siri Recap, meanwhile, creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. Both of these features will launch in beta later this year, Apple says. The company has outlined a thorough privacy strategy around these features, too. 

Combined with the launch of Siri AI, Siri Recap and Live Rewind are the biggest steps yet toward Apple turning the Apple Watch into a full-fledged AI wearable — something I’m really excited to see play out.

9to5Mac’s Take

Who should upgrade to the Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4? I think this is one of the most substantial upgrades we’ve seen in recent years. If you’re in the Series 9 or Ultra 2 crowd (or earlier), I’d seriously consider making the jump. If you have a newer Apple Watch, it really boils down to how much you care about the new health features.

On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 seem like small updates. They don’t reinvent the form factor (although the new colors and material options are fantastic).

Instead, it’s what’s happening underneath that makes the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 so interesting. Apple has focused on making the watch considerably more capable at what it already does best: serving as an always-on companion that can monitor your heart, sleep, and activity. Oh, and it keeps you connected to friends, family, and the rest of the outside world.

The new Health Sensing System is the foundation for all of this. It fundamentally changes how much your Apple Watch knows about you throughout the day.

Crucially, Apple didn’t just increase the frequency of heart rate readings and put the burden on you to decipher all that added data. The new hardware ties together with watchOS 27 to provide meaningful insight into your daily life, including the promising Readiness app and a more capable Vitals app.

The story is even more exciting when you factor in the Siri Recap and Live Rewind features coming later this year. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 not only know more about you now than ever before, but they will also help you keep up with the world around you.

Taken as a whole, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer the clearest indication yet of what the future holds for Apple’s most important wearable.

title: The iPhone Duo didn’t reinvent Android foldables, but I fear the copycats anyway
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is here and, shocker, it didn’t exactly reinvent the foldable, but the iPhone Duo did get some of the most important aspects right, and will give the Android side of the conversation some things to work on too. 9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is here and, shocker, it didn’t exactly reinvent the foldable, but the iPhone Duo did get some of the most important aspects right, and will give the Android side of the conversation some things to work on too.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Look, I promise we’ll stop talking about the iPhone Duo at some point. We’re not 9to5Mac, but Apple’s first foldable is a big deal for the Android side of the industry too. It’s not every day that an entirely new form factor built up by Android brands gets co-opted by the only real competitor. 

And, despite Android’s several-year head start, Apple is immediately putting up a fierce competition with its iPhone Duo.

	

It’s a polished foldable across the board. A smart design with aspect ratios that should prove useful – and, based on the Fold 8’s popularity, resonate among customers – and a package that seems to deliver on everything it needs to. It’s thicker and heavier than basically every other current Android foldable, but it’s also not so far out of the ordinary as to be uncompetitive. Early reactions have been positive, though I’m certainly curious to see what people think after the typical Apple event psychosis wears off.

But, as good as the Duo looks, I think the biggest thing to walk away with is that Apple is not reinventing the foldable. It’s been speculated for years now that Apple would somehow crack open the formula on how to build a foldable in ways that no Android brand had figured out and, based on what’s been shown off so far, that’s simply not the case.

On the hardware side, Apple doesn’t seem to outdo existing hardware in any particularly meaningful ways. The matte display is the thing that has my attention most, as it seems to lessen even the visual appearance of a crease to essentially nothing – though, without that, I bet it’d be similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Oppo Find N6. But even that display doesn’t seem flawless, with the glossy dot over the selfie camera immediately catching my attention. Under-display cameras are already a tech that’s been shown to be of dubious worth, and with this visual oddity at play, I’m pretty surprised Apple adopted this one at all.

via Brian Tong
via Brian Tong
iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well

The software is where even I expected Apple to figure out ideas for a foldable beyond what we’ve seen but, really, there wasn’t much.

Split-screen looks mostly akin to the Pixel Fold, though with the two halves treated as independent by default and allowing you to go to the homescreen to grab another app. That feels very intuitive, even if Android has the same core functionality through its taskbar. The ability to put video windows on top of other apps looks useful and more polished than existing split-screen or picture-in-picture options on Android, but it’s still not exactly groundbreaking. 

The most attention-grabbing additions in Apple’s software come from a neat animation that shows up when you open or close the device – almost certainly set to be copied in future software updates on Android devices – and a rethinking of navigation.

Apple is moving app controls and the status bar to the side of the UI rather than the top and bottom where they’re resided for ages now. It gives me mixed feelings. The utility of offloading those controls to the side of the display to make vertical content feel more at home on the wider aspect ratio makes sense, but it also looks wildly ugly to me, or unbalanced at the very least.

All of this is to say, Apple didn’t break any new ground here, and they still have to deal with many of the same problems.

Like every existing foldable, Apple has some different ideas to add into the core experience, but that core experience is essentially the same – it’s just based on iOS this time. Android “got it right” in terms of that core experience, and now everyone has a chance to sit down and think about where to take it next. In a way, it reminds me of the whole app drawer situation. Android got this right years ago, and Apple brought in its own version that’s the same core idea, just different (and much worse, but I digress).

What worries me is the idea that Android manufacturers are going to rush to copy what Apple has put out. 

There’s nothing on the iPhone Duo, at least not yet, that feels worth copying – except maybe that aforementioned animation. The sidebar setup, for instance, acknowledges a problem that these new form factors are facing. Modern smartphones are all tall and narrow slabs, so wide designs aren’t a thought for developers. By offloading everything to the side, Apple is presenting a solution for the lack of space for content that devices like Fold 8 have to give up for the sake of top and bottom bars. I’m just personally not sure it’s the right solution. As just one example, this UI decision sounds awful for anyone who uses their phone in their left hand (which, hello, that’s me). At least the top and bottom bars are equally a little bit uncomfortable for everyone.

It’s a bold new chapter in the foldable market, and Apple is surely set to sell a lot of these. I’m perhaps most surprised that it’s competitively priced – cheaper than Samsung’s top foldable, too! On top of that, I think the Duo will be a net-positive for Android foldables in the long run. title: Today’s NYT Strands Hints, Answers and Help for Sept. 17, #928
snippet: Here are hints and the answers for today’s NYT Strands puzzle for Sept. 17, 2026.
fullText:
Looking for the most recent NYT Strands puzzle answers? CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

Strands is like a word find game, but without the list of words to find. Sometimes I see the theme and begin recognizing the answers right away. But for those times when I can’t seem to manage this, there’s a loophole: Strands lets you make as many words of four or more letters as you want. For every three of those words you find, the puzzle will highlight one of the answers. You’re still going to have to unscramble that answer, though, which can be very tough.

I go into depth about the rules for Strands in this story. 

Today’s puzzle has a really fun category for those of us who grew up reading newspapers, especially on Sundays. Read on for hints and all the answers.

Hint for today’s Strands puzzle

Today’s Strands theme is: A little comic relief.

If that doesn’t help you, here’s a clue: Doonesbury or Cathy.

Clue words to unlock in-game hints

Your goal is to find hidden words that fit the puzzle’s theme. If you’re stuck, find any words you can. Every time you find three words of four letters or more, Strands will reveal one of the theme words. These are the words I used to get those hints, but any words of four or more letters that you find will work:

MUST, FUNNY, CLAP, CLAPS, BLOCK, NUTS, STUN, CONE, CONES

These are the answers that tie into the theme. The goal of the puzzle is to find them all, including the “spangram,” a theme word that reaches from one side of the puzzle to the other. When you have all of them (I originally thought there were always eight, but learned that the number can vary), every letter on the board will be used. Here are the nonspangram answers:

ZIPPY, ZITS, MUTTS, BLONDIE, PEANUTS, PICKLES

Today’s Strands spangram

The completed NYT Strands puzzle for Sept. 17, 2026.NYT/Screenshot by CNET

Today’s Strands spangram is THEFUNNYPAGES. To find it, start with the T that’s the first letter on the far left, and wind down, over and then down again.

Toughest Strands puzzles

Here are some of the Strands topics I’ve found to be the toughest.

#1: Dated slang. Maybe you didn’t even use this lingo when it was cool. Toughest word: PHAT.

#2: Thar she blows! I guess marine biologists might ace this one. Toughest word: BALEEN or RIGHT. 

#3: Off the hook. Again, it helps to know a lot about sea creatures. Sorry, Charlie. Toughest word: BIGEYE or SKIPJACK.

title: Photographer Tyler Stalman reviews the iPhone 18 Pro’s new camera with variable aperture
snippet: Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here’s what he had to say about the iPhone 18 Pro’s new variable aperture, photographic styles, Apple Reference Image, and more. more…
fullText:
Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here’s what he had to say about the iPhone 18 Pro’s new variable aperture, photographic styles, Apple Reference Image, and more.

Stalman explores the iPhone 18 Pro camera’s variable aperture

Although this year’s iPhone 18 Pro introduces many new features, including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, it is fair to say that the biggest camera upgrade is its new variable aperture system.

Also new this year are updates to Cinematic mode, expanded Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Image, and further improvements to the Camera app’s pro controls.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman published a review of all of the iPhone 18 Pro’s new hardware and software features, adding to the wave of reviews that went live as the embargo lifted, including ours.

Stalman notes that although he enjoyed last year’s Cosmic Orange color on his iPhone 17 Pro, it tended to appear in reflections when shooting through windows. For this reason, he says pro photographers might want to stick to Burgundy or Black, as they are less likely to cast unwanted color into photos or videos.

He also notes right off the bat that his review compares the iPhone 18 Pro’s cameras to those of the iPhone 15 Pro, while the video itself was shot almost entirely on an iPhone 17 Pro.

When it comes to the main camera upgrade, which is the new variable aperture, Stalman says its addition is “one step along the way to making (the iPhone) a serious camera.”

He also notes that the wider f/1.48 aperture lets more light reach the sensor, which can help keep ISO lower in low-light conditions and reduce the need for Night mode.

This part of the review includes a few very cool-looking shots of the iris mechanism opening and closing, and Stalman points out that Apple’s implementation is somewhat unusual, with the aperture blades positioned above the primary lens element rather than deeper inside the lens, as they typically are on traditional camera lenses.

Stalman also says that the iPhone 18 Pro’s 4x zoom (also present in last year’s iPhone) is a nice improvement over the iPhone 16 Pro’s 5x zoom, which could at times feel a little too tight.

And speaking of going too far, he quickly touches on the new AI-powered editing tools, such as Clean Up, Extend, and Reframe, noting that although they are technically impressive and quite convincing, they can make such significant changes that the resulting image no longer feels entirely authentic to the original photo.

When it comes to the iPhone 18 Pro’s new texture options, including Soft Skin, Glow, and Film, Stalman demonstrates each effect by moving its intensity from 0 to 100. As for his impressions, he says Soft Skin does a subtle job of reducing skin detail without simply blurring it, while Glow adds a diffused highlight effect similar to a black mist filter.

He is also impressed by the Film effect’s grain and halation, though he wishes Apple offered more control over the amount of grain.

The review also touches on Apple Reference Image, the iPhone’s Cinematic mode (and how Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic footage), as well as the new Apple Log 2, and is naturally peppered with photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.

title: This iOS 27 bug temporarily freezes your iPhone … and it’s going viral on social media
snippet: Just a matter of days after iOS 27 has been released to the public, people have already discovered a way to temporarily brick your phone with a quick series of swipes on the home screen. And it’s starting to going viral on social media as some kind of iPhone prank to do on your friends. Luckily, it is only a software soft-lock and you can easily get out of this temporarily bricked state by force rebooting your phone. Here’s how … more…
fullText:
Just a matter of days after iOS 27 has been released to the public, people have already discovered a way to temporarily brick your phone with a quick series of swipes on the home screen. And it’s starting to going viral on social media as some kind of iPhone prank to do on your friends.

Luckily, it is only a software soft-lock and you can easily get out of this temporarily bricked state by force rebooting your phone. Here’s how …

These kind of soft-locks have existed in various iOS versions in the past, and Apple usually gets round to fixing them eventually. Sometimes, they have necessitated complex sequence of taps and gestures to trigger the bug. In this case, it’s pretty trivial to get into the busted state. 

On a phone running iOS 27, go to the Home Screen, then pull down from the top-left corner as if you were opening Notification Center. Almost immediately after, way before the Notification Center has finished sliding down, pull down from the right-hand corner to open Control Center. Then, dismiss Control Center and you can see if your phone has entered the borked state.

Usually, when this happens the lock screen buttons for Camera and Torch get stuck at the top of the screen. But the big-tell tale sign is you can no longer swipe between home screens, and if you open apps, taps don’t reliably register on UI elements so you can’t really navigate around the phone anymore.

If you try and hold the side button to get to the slide to power off screen, the slider doesn’t respond to your swipe gesture.

Luckily, this is all completely harmless and the solution to get out the bricked state is to force-reboot the phone. That causes the phone to shut down and restart:

To force reboot a modern iPhone, press the volume up button once, press the volume down button once, then hold the side button down until the Apple logo appears. Your phone will then reboot and be back to normal. 

If you try and reproduce this glitch, and you can’t get it to work for you, you might need to repeat the swipes a couple times. It’s not hard to do, but there’s only small window of time where it works. I can reliably reproduce it within about two or three attempts on my iPhone Air running iOS 27.0, and it still happens on the just-released iOS 27.2 beta as well.

Here’s a screen recording of me reproducing the bug; swipe from top-left, then quickly swipe from top-right:

title: Apple Card has three new and improved features in iOS 27
snippet: Apple Card gets even better in iOS 27, with new features like a recurring transactions section to help you stay on top of regular charges. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple Card gets even better in iOS 27, with new features like a recurring transactions section to help you stay on top of regular charges. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Recurring transactions section

iOS 27 adds a brand new ‘Recurring’ section to Apple Card in the Wallet app. You’ll find it inside the three-dot menu in the upper right corner when viewing your Apple Card.

The Recurring section is a new go-to hub for seeing all Apple Card transactions that occur regularly.

You can view recurring transactions on a calendar view by month, or see a chronological list of upcoming transactions.

Apple explains how this works: “Dates and amounts shown are predicted based on your transaction history and may not be exact.” In my usage, the accuracy has been pretty spot-on.

Plenty of services offer to help you gain awareness of all your subscriptions. And now, Apple Card can do that without you needing to share financial data with third parties.

#2: Notifications for upcoming charges

Related to the new recurring transactions feature, iOS 27 adds a new type of notifications you can choose to enable or disable.

When viewing your Apple Card, tap the ‘Notifications’ option inside the three-dot menu and you’ll see an addition: ‘Upcoming Transactions.’

Based on your transaction history, Apple Card can predict when new recurring charges will go through and notify you ahead of time that they’re coming.

It’s a convenient way to stay apprised of your spending and subscriptions. And if you don’t want those extra notifications, they’re easy to turn off.

#3: Redesigned Apple Pay interface

iOS 27 (left) vs iOS 26 (right)

Apple Card users will also benefit from the redesigned Apple Pay checkout UI in iOS 27.

Any time you use Apple Pay on a website or in an app, you’ll now see a refreshed, better organized, more informative checkout screen.

The new design makes it easy to check at a glance that details like shipping and billing addresses are all accurate. And if you decide not to use your Apple Card for a given transaction, switching between cards is now easier than ever too.

title: Having Trouble Loading Pizzas Into the Oven? Your Peel May Be the Problem
snippet: I tried a $26 sliding pizza peel that promises smoother launches.
fullText:
Home pizza ovens are on a tear and present an excellent alternative to hot indoor cooking.

																			CNET
												
			
				

Chances are, if you own a pizza oven, have stood near a pizza oven or have uttered the words “pizza oven” in the vicinity of your phone, it’s likely that the almighty algorithm has delivered up a steady stream of pizza oven accessories, from pizza oven stands to sizzler platters to pizza peels in every style and shape.

If you have cursed in the vicinity of your phone while trying to launch a pizza into your pizza oven without inadvertently creating a calzone, chances are even better that Big Internet Brother has targeted you for a sliding pizza peel. If, after dozens of practice launches, you haven’t mastered the art of the traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel, even with all-powerful semolina flour gliders, you may be very tempted by the ease promised by such a tool as a sliding pizza peel.

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Pizza Ovens, Tested by CNET					

							

		

But is it worth it? Or is it just the Temu-niverse capitalizing on your desire for a homemade pizza that doesn’t come with a side of anxiety and despair? Reader, the temptation was too strong. I checked one out, and here’s the lowdown on what you can expect from a sliding pizza peel.

How does a sliding pizza peel work?

A sliding pizza peel costs $30 to $40 on Amazon.Pamela Vachon/CNET

A sliding pizza peel is essentially a lightweight wooden pizza peel with a manual conveyor belt attached. Rather than thrusting a stationary peel under your entire pie, you only need a small edge of maneuverability to start. Once the sliding peel gets a little purchase on the raw pizza dough, you pull the cloth slide toward you by its handle while pushing the wooden board underneath. 

To launch the pizza with a sliding pizza peel, reverse the process: Use the handle on the cloth glider to push, sliding the pizza into the oven while pulling the sturdy board out from underneath it.

Cloth, you say? Well, not exactly. The conveyor mechanism moves like fabric, but think of it more like a nonstick baking mat. Many are made of woven fiberglass with a polytetrafluoroethylene coating, which is nonstick but still grips enough to hold raw or cooked pizza dough. It’s frankly like a flimsier Silpat or not unlike an oilcloth table covering.

PTFE, in case you’re wondering, is related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Yes, we’ve worked hard to avoid PFAS; however, the material’s pliability doesn’t encourage chipping, and it is also replaceable. The wooden board itself admittedly also spares every expense without the heavy lifting required of other wooden pizza peels — this is made from raw, lightweight bamboo. 

Sliding pizza peel best practices

I practiced with naked dough.Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a sliding pizza peel may seem like a cure-all, if, like me, you adore what your pizza oven offers but still struggle with pizza peel mechanics, it still requires practiceof its own —and caution. As with more traditional pizza peels, it cannot undo other mistakes, such as poorly constructed, too warm pizza dough or an overloaded pie. You can still calzone-ify your pizza, even with a sliding pizza peel.

Unlike a traditional pizza peel, which lets you push and pull simultaneously, the sliding pizza peel’s primary handle is also very short, meaning you kind of have to get (uncomfortably) close to the mouth of the oven to use it.

The fact that none of these seemingly magic wands are produced or branded by any major pizza oven manufacturer should serve as a caution. (Pizza oven manufacturers probably just want you to become a bona fide pizzaiolo, confidently using the legitimate tools of the trade; they are clearly not trying to encourage the use of these cheap devices.)

Various sliding pizza peels are purportedly heat-resistant up to a certain temperature (which varies). Many pizza ovens, however, can reach temperatures much hotter than those sliding peels are designed for.

Loading a raw pie into the oven is one of the trickiest parts of at-home pizza making.Pamela Vachon/CNET

More than one user on various online pizza oven forums reported that the nonstick belt of a sliding pizza peel melted onto the hot pizza stone. Others, however, called the device an absolute game changer. Either way, using a sliding pizza peel requires you to launch quickly, which again requires practice, probably best done outside your actual pizza oven. (Your oven-oven with a removable pizza stone? A much lower-stakes practice arena.)

My experience with a sliding pizza peel

Because of the peel’s modest length, you have to get uncomfortably close to the oven during launch.Pamela Vachon/CNET

I have been an enthusiastic pizza oven user since one came into my life, but I still haven’t mastered the mechanics of either a traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel. I slightly prefer metal, but either way, pizza attempt number one always results in a folded disaster. My crime, apparently, is wanting the kind of thin pizza crust a 20-year-old New Yorker demands. The thinner the pizza, the harder to launch.

I can attest that the sliding pizza peel did make it easy to pull the pizza off the cutting board where I shaped the dough and applied toppings. Despite feeling cheaply made, the mechanics are inarguable. I achieved a crust thinness I truly couldn’t with the other models.

While you have to get close to the heat to deposit it, I haven’t earned any burns or scars from trying. Repeated launches in a very hot pizza oven also didn’t seem to affect the fabric slide, but then again, I was prepared to move extremely fast to avoid a crisis—and to get away from the heat.

Success, if not exactly centered.Pamela Vachion/CNET

In case it merits saying, a sliding pizza peel is entirely unnecessary for pulling pizza out of a pizza oven. In fact, I would caution against it since it really relies on setting the peel down on the pizza stone, never mind the fact that you really have to get your hand inside the oven in the starting position for pulling a pizza onto it. Once a pizza is fully cooked and the dough is sturdy, even a thin pizza can be collected with a more traditional pizza peel anyhow.

A traditional pizza peel is still best for pulling pies from the oven.Pamela Vachon/CNET

The verdict on a sliding pizza peel? Proceed with caution. And practice.

Ultimately, the average price of sliding pizza peels available online is about $30. Even with mixed reviews, it’s a fairly low-stakes gamble to see whether one improves how often you use your big-ticket pizza oven.

Design and colors

Apple debuted a striking new design with last year’s iPhone 17 Pro lineup, including a full-width camera bump plateau and a two-tone back.

In my review, I described the changes as “polarizing.” I said the camera plateau along the back was Apple finally embracing the camera bump, but that I’d prefer consistency between the aluminum and glass cutout on the back.

I think that has been the general public reaction, too. I heard from a lot of iPhone 17 Pro buyers who didn’t like the two-tone design and opted to cover it up with a case when they might have otherwise gone case-less.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has debuted a new color-matched back design. That is, the glass cutout on the back now matches the color of the aluminum, for the most part. It looks fantastic. You can still see and feel the seam where the glass meets the aluminum, but the overall appearance here is much better.

The iPhone 18 Pro is available in four colors: burgundy, glacier, silver, and black. If I had to pick a “flagship” color for this year, I’d say it’s burgundy. It’s not as bright and flashy as last year’s cosmic orange, but it’s unlike anything we’ve seen on an iPhone before. It’s a beautiful mix between a deep red and purple, shifting depending on lighting.

Meanwhile, glacier is a light blue that I’d describe as similar to, but slightly lighter than, the sierra blue of the iPhone 13 Pro. However, unlike the sky blue MacBook Air that can easily pass for silver, it is unmistakably blue.

Of all the iPhone 17 Pro colors, the silver was most afflicted by the two-tone back design. Apple’s signature silver aluminum design was marred by the white glass on the back. This year, the silver iPhone 18 Pro looks stunning thanks to Apple color-matching the silver aluminum to the glass.

And for those who were upset the iPhone 17 Pro wasn’t available in black, I’m happy to report that the black iPhone 18 Pro is the darkest Pro iPhone that Apple has ever made. There’s no mistaking it for a space gray or midnight. It’s black.

My review units are the iPhone 18 Pro in glacier and the iPhone 18 Pro Max in burgundy. I adore the burgundy and it stands out as my favorite this year. Glacier is nice, but doesn’t have quite enough “pop” for my liking — especially after last year’s cosmic orange.

Size

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are both heavier than their predecessors, while the overall footprint (including thickness) has not changed this year:

I’m glad Apple isn’t shying away from making the phones heavier if it means better cameras, battery life, and performance. That said, there’s a limit to how heavy a “Max” phone can be while still being comfortable to hold, and with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, I think we’ve reached it.

The added weight over its predecessor is obvious the moment you pick up the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It’s right at the edge of what I’m willing to carry, and for me, that’s enough reason to choose the iPhone 18 Pro instead.

Dynamic Island

The other big change with the iPhone 18 Pro design is the Dynamic Island. The new Dynamic Island is around 25% smaller than before. This was made possible by moving the infrared camera for Face ID beneath the display, with Apple using a section of brighter pixels to let just enough of the infrared light through for Face ID.

The smaller Dynamic Island is immediately noticeable. You can clearly see the additional space between the Dynamic Island and things in your iPhone’s status bar, like the time and cellular signal bars.

Where it really shines, though, is through the software optimizations Apple has made to take advantage of it.

The headlining change is that you can now have three Live Activities at the same time. You can have one bigger Live Activity in the middle, with smaller ones on either side.

In my testing, what I’ve actually appreciated most is what happens when you have two Live Activities running at the same time. Thanks to the smaller Dynamic Island, the second Live Activity that appears on the right side can now show more information.

Here’s what having two Live Activities looked like on the iPhone 17 Pro:

And here’s what it looks like on iPhone 18 Pro:

Instead of having to long-press to view additional information, the smaller Dynamic Island means you can now see that right in the Live Activity itself. It’s a useful change that I’ve already come to appreciate over the last week.

I haven’t noticed any downsides to the Face ID infrared camera moving under the display. Face ID still works just as well as it did before. In bright sunlight, you can see the infrared camera below the display. In normal lighting, however, it’s indistinguishable from the rest of the display.

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro (right)

Thermals and performance

The iPhone 17 Pro marked a huge leap for iPhone performance thanks to a completely revamped thermal management system with an Apple-designed vapor chamber. This year, Apple has made another jump.

The iPhone 18 Pro is powered by the A20 Pro chip. The memory now sits side-by-side with the chip, rather than physically on top of the chip itself. This new packaging technology means the A20 Pro chip can attach directly to the iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber.

Apple says the vapor chamber inside the iPhone 18 Pro has 3x the surface area of the iPhone 17 Pro’s vapor chamber. It is also using new materials, including more thermally conductive graphite and nano-twin copper that moves heat away from the display.

Benchmarks only tell a fraction of the story, but in my testing, they matched, and in some cases even exceeded, Apple’s claims. The iPhone 18 Pro’s A20 Pro CPU consistently came in between 22 and 27% faster than the A19 Pro, while the GPU landed between 40 and 45% faster.

I did not expect such a dramatic year-over-year leap in performance and thermals. To have two consecutive years of this level of change is an incredible feat by Apple’s teams.

We’ve come a long way from the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro. Both of those phones suffered from poor thermals, leading to throttled performance and the devices themselves getting uncomfortably hot to the touch.

Three years ago, thermals were the iPhone’s biggest weakness. With the iPhone 18 Pro, they’ve become one of its biggest strengths.

Battery life

Apple’s stats around battery life haven’t been particularly useful in the past. After all, who is using their iPhone to watch 45 hours of continuous video playback? Regardless, here are the stats for this year and other recent iPhone generations.

Where applicable, these figures are for the eSIM-only models sold in the US and a handful of other markets. Apple says versions with a physical SIM card get about two hours less video playback.

Apple touts that the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the “largest increase in battery life ever on iPhone.”

This year, Apple is also providing a new “typical use” battery life measurement for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple says this number is based on a “combination of passive and active use of a variety of applications, including but not limited to messaging, photos, music, social media, video streaming, games, web browsing, and navigation.”

iPhone 18 Pro typical use battery life: Up to 24 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max typical use battery life: Up to 30 hours

It’s going to be interesting to see how that “typical use” stat evolves over the years, but I’m glad Apple is finally offering useful battery metrics.

During my review period, I’ve primarily been using the iPhone 18 Pro Max. I’m easily able to make it through a day and a half on a charge, starting each day around 6 a.m. and not needing to plug in until lunchtime the following day at the earliest. I’ve spent less time with the smaller Pro, but in the days I used it, it comfortably lasted a full day.

Camera

Apple’s headlining change for the iPhone 18 Pro is the addition of a new variable aperture 48MP Fusion Main camera. It’s the first time the iPhone has featured a variable aperture camera. As Apple explained during the iPhone 18 Pro launch, the design consists of six laser-cut blades that transition between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0.

There are really two iPhone 18 Pro camera stories.

The first is for everyone who leaves the camera on Auto. The variable aperture works without you touching anything, and in my testing it made a difference in two situations: at night, where the camera opens to ƒ/1.48 and gathers more light, and in scenes with something close to the lens, where it stops down to ƒ/4 and keeps both the subject and background sharp.

In ordinary daylight, the aperture is still moving, often to ƒ/4, but on a typical landscape scene, the change in aperture makes little visible difference compared with the iPhone 17 Pro, since there’s nothing close enough for the extra depth of field to matter. The photos themselves do look different, but that’s down to the new image pipeline, which I’ll get to below, not the lens.

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right)

No Night mode

iPhone 17 Pro Max: ƒ/1.78, 1/15s, ISO 12,500

iPhone 18 Pro Max: ƒ/1.48, 1/15s, ISO 10,000

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right)

Night mode

iPhone 17 Pro Max: ƒ/1.78, 0.5s, ISO 3,200

iPhone 18 Pro Max: ƒ/1.48, 0.5s, ISO 2,500

The night gain is the easiest to measure. Across my comparisons, the iPhone 18 Pro consistently used a lower ISO than the iPhone 17 Pro in the same scene at the same shutter speed. In this example, both cameras shot at 1/15 second, but the iPhone 18 Pro used ISO 10,000 compared with ISO 12,500 on the iPhone 17 Pro. The wider ƒ/1.48 aperture lets in more light, reducing how much the camera needs to amplify the signal and helping cut down on noise. You can really notice it in the detail of the trees and the sky. 

For Night Mode, capture times are slightly shorter thanks to the ƒ/1.48 aperture. Taking a Night Mode picture is often a test of your hand stability, so anything Apple can do to reduce that time is greatly appreciated. 

Depth of field is the other half of the aperture story. A wide aperture like ƒ/1.48 keeps a narrower slice of the scene in focus, while a smaller aperture like ƒ/4 keeps much more of it sharp, front to back.

On an iPhone, that difference is most noticeable when your subject is close to the camera. And importantly, this is real optical depth of field, not the computational blur that iPhone creates in Portrait mode.

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left, ƒ/1.78) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right, ƒ/4.0)

In this example shot of a buoy, the iPhone 18 Pro stopped down to ƒ/4 on its own. The buoy, concrete, and far pier are all sharp. The same shot on the iPhone 17 Pro, fixed at ƒ/1.78, kept the buoy sharp but let the background go slightly soft. The same logic applies to group photos, where stopping down can help keep the back row as sharp as the front.

In this dog example, I manually switched between ƒ/1.48 and ƒ/4. Look at the treeline and its reflection — sharp at ƒ/4, soft at ƒ/1.48, while Blake stays sharp in both:

iPhone 18 Pro Max, ƒ/1.48 (left) and ƒ/4 (right)

The second story is for pro photographers. For that crowd, the iPhone 18 Pro unlocks a wider array of new creative opportunities. You can set the aperture yourself, enabling things like six-point starbursts on streetlights at ƒ/4. Pro controls also add manual shutter speed, white balance, and a live histogram, and the whole panel is customizable so you can choose which settings you want quick access to.

Personally, I fall into the first category. I am not a pro photographer. I rely on Apple’s automatic settings to capture the best possible photo in almost every scenario. I think the iPhone 18 Pro does exactly that, just like the iPhone 17 Pro did before it. The difference is that the variable aperture means there’s more happening in the background to make my photos better, and I don’t have to worry about any of it. That’s what I want from my iPhone.

More on iPhone 18 Pro camera

Apple touts an upgraded computational image pipeline for “sharper, more detailed shots.” In my testing, I found a subtle but noticeable difference, particularly with the 48MP Main camera. Pictures from the iPhone 18 Pro are consistently a touch brighter than the same shots from the iPhone 17 Pro, as you can see below. 

The iPhone 18 Pro also offers Photographic Styles 3 for texture and grain control. As someone who loves Photographic Styles, I’m glad to see Apple continuing to improve the feature after last year’s major update.

A few other iPhone 18 Pro camera tidbits:

Audio Mix can now isolate music in videos.

The Cinematic effect for videos can now be applied after the fact. This is a fantastic change, as you can now decide after shooting a video whether the effect works for the scene.

Timelapses now support 4K resolution and Dolby Vision HDR.

Here are a few more sample shots from the iPhone 18 Pro Max compared to the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Both phones were set to the Standard Photographic Style for every comparison in this review.

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right)

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right)

iPhone 17 Pro Max (left) vs iPhone 18 Pro Max (right)

Pricing

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB of storage. The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB. That’s a $100 price hike for the base configurations over last year’s models. The price increase, however, is more dramatic as you upgrade storage capacities.

For example, last year’s 1TB iPhone 17 Pro was $1,499 and the 1TB iPhone 17 Pro Max was $1,599. This year, the 1TB iPhone 18 Pro is $1,799 and the 1TB iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,899.

The pricing suggests Apple ate some margin on the 256GB and 512GB configurations and made it back on the higher tiers. I think a lot of iPhone buyers can get by with 256GB of storage, and the majority can comfortably live with 512GB. It’s people who need 1TB or 2TB who are most affected by these price hikes.

9to5Mac’s Take

Last year, Apple drew a clear line in the sand for what it thought the iPhone Pro should be. The iPhone 17 Pro was the best, most capable, most unapologetically “Pro” phone Apple had ever released. It made design tradeoffs in favor of offering significant upgrades in performance, thermal headroom, and camera capability.

Now, the question is: What happens the year after Apple gets the formula right?

As it turns out, the answer is simple: more of the same. Apple has doubled down on its strategy. The iPhone 18 Pro takes the foundation of the iPhone 17 Pro and pushes it even further. There is a massive leap in performance, the camera is more capable, the Dynamic Island is smaller, and battery life is even better. That, of course, comes at the cost of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max being even heavier than their predecessors.

Ultimately, if you’re using the iPhone 17 Pro right now, there’s little reason to upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro. If you’re using an iPhone 16 Pro or earlier, I’d say now’s a great time to make the leap.

I’ve gone this whole review without mentioning the iPhone Duo, which is set to launch next month. If the iPhone Duo is the new kid on the block, the iPhone 18 Pro is a familiar old friend, and I mean that in the best way possible.

title: Every single new feature in Android 17 QPR1 [Video]
snippet: Get ready, Android 17 QPR1 is now available, and it might be a refresh that hardware holdouts hope is going to give them some great new features – here is everything new. more…
fullText:
Get ready, Android 17 QPR1 is now available, and it might be a refresh that hardware holdouts hope is going to give them some great new features – here is everything new.

Just a few weeks after the Pixel 11 started shipping, we now have a fresh update to install and run on your new phone, or any device from the Pixel 6 through to the newest additions. We are not getting huge changes here, just a few tweaks, some more refinements, mostly quality of life changes.

If you want more, the Pixel Drop for September 2026 adds a little more flavor to what is, in all honesty, a very small update by the standards of Quarterly Platform Releases. As noted, most of the new functionality is very minimal at best or not notable at worst. You’ll probably notice that this update is heavily weighted toward cosmetic changes. That’s mostly just a symptom of Android hitting a bit of a functionality ceiling as of late.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

UI changes

Core user interface changes are part and parcel of any Android update, as things get tweaked and tuned to help improve the cohesion of specific sections and subsections. All UI changes we have tracked relate to commonly used areas and features within Android 17 QPR1, with changes over the previous base Android 17 and 16 builds and releases noted.

Lockscreen animation slide-ins improved

Google has tuned one of the key lockscreen UI portions with a vastly improved slide-in animation for media player controls while your phone is locked. When you have something playing, and your phone is locked, tapping the power button or the screen causes the media player UI to slide up into view rather than being static on your display.

It’s super clean and gives this already fun section just a little more life per Material 3 Expressive’s aim for more playful UI interactions.

Pixel Search settings in App List settings

Although live on the Pixel 11, older Pixels will get access to the new Pixel Search settings option within App list settings. This gives you options for the search bar at the top of the App drawer, so you can tune the experience to show suggestions, apps, and full web search, and adjust whether the keyboard appears automatically.

Stashed media player in Quick Settings

If you have multiple media apps open or are using multiple at the same time, Android 17 QPR1 now stashes these within the Quick Settings panel so you are able to switch quickly while still making it easy to manage one at a time. This change is also present on the lockscreen.

Usability changes

Android 17 QPR1 includes a host of usability enhancements aimed at making everyday device interactions smoother and more intuitive. This section details these core changes to the Android 17 QPR1 experience, which may also include some new functionalities.

Predictive back gesture in Quick Settings

Predictive back or a close approximation is coming to the Quick Setting panel, as you’ll get a visual indicator of what will happen when using back gestures. Instead of just minimizing, you’ll see the notifications appear when fully expanded (if there are any). Then, going back once more will show the homescreen before you release the gesture.

This is a better implementation than in previous versions, as the section would just collapse with no indication of where you’d end up.

Keyboard QS tile

Android 17 QPR1 has a new Keyboard tile that you can add to Quick Settings. If you add and activate it, it gives you the pop-up menu for your installed keyboards, allowing you to quickly switch anywhere within your device system. Long pressing opens up the Keyboard apps section and allows you to enable or disable any installed apps. If you have multiple keyboard applications, this might be a really neat, quick tool to switch when required.

New mobile data pop-up

Easily one of the best new features in Android 17 QPR1 is the ability to dismiss the annoying “Turn on mobile data” pop-up that usually appears every time you want to make a change. When you turn mobile data off and then re-enable it, there’s a new checkbox labeled “Do not ask me again,” so you won’t keep getting prompted to turn on mobile data if you have disabled it momentarily.

Some applications with multiple actions and shortcuts offer split panels to reduce on-screen clutter – especially on smaller displays. When you long-press an app icon such as Pocket Casts, the default app actions, including widgets, remove, app info, pause, and bubble, will be visible. A new “Shortcuts” toggle lets you tap to access quick in-app shortcuts and add them to your homescreen. Not all apps will have these options.

Screen recording adjustments

In Android 17 QPR1, Google has adjusted the menu so that the last-used app is now the default option, and the dropdown menu starts with “single app” selected. If you were to tap “start” immediately, the most recent app would be selected and recorded. Previously, this defaulted to “Entire Screen.”

Cosmetic changes

Alongside features, Android 17 QPR1 focuses on some cosmetic or visual changes to the experience you’ll have with your Pixel phone. Most are merely updates to areas that may have been overlooked or recently added in previous software versions.

New QS edit tile icon

If you want to edit your Quick Settings tiles, there is a new icon that combines the pencil icon with some tiles to show you how the enhanced system works.

When you view sections in Settings, the spacing increases to pre-Android 17 levels, making things feel less cramped, albeit with fewer options on screen. You’ll have to scroll a little more.

Gemini Intelligence boot logo

We’re not actually sure how widespread this is, given that Gemini Intelligence isn’t technically expected to come to older Pixel phones now. Some may see the Gemini Intelligence logo when rebooting or powering on their devices, but only on the Pixel 10 and newer. It’s already live on Pixel 11 devices.

Many of the pop-up menus on your Pixel will be smaller with Android 17 QPR1. This is prominent with the Wallpaper and style pop-up and some of the mini menus.

New app icons

Google has updated the entire suite of default app icons, including Settings and various other first-party apps like Clock, Calculator, and Recorder, to fit the new “Pixel style.” 

Improved animations

Some further attention has been paid to animations added over the last couple of years, with even more bounce when using Quick Settings. Tiles respond to slide speed, exhibiting overshoot and easing back into position. Some other animations have a little more bounce, but it’s most visible here.

Increased system blur

Not to be confused with Liquid Glass, Google’s system blur effect is more prominent in more areas with marginally more glassy visuals in the app drawer, volume slider sidebar, the power menu, and app pop-ups. It’s not completely frosted, but has increased opacity.

App notification dot visual update

If you have enabled notification dots in Android 17 QPR1, you will see a new Dynamic Color-styled outline that helps the dot stand out from icons.

title: AppZapper 3000: ‘The uninstaller Apple forgot’ returns for the modern Mac era
snippet: AppZapper is one of the first Mac apps I bought when I switched from PC to Mac in 2009. Coming from Windows, OS X lacked an obvious solution for thoroughly uninstalling software. The answer, of course, is dragging an app from the Applications folder to the Trash. But what about all the extra cruft that apps leave behind? AppZapper handled it. This week, the app returned from a long hiatus to introduce a brand-new version of “the uninstaller Apple forgot” with AppZapper 3000. more…
fullText:
AppZapper is one of the first Mac apps I bought when I switched from PC to Mac in 2009. Coming from Windows, OS X lacked an obvious solution for thoroughly uninstalling software. 

The answer, of course, is dragging an app from the Applications folder to the Trash. But what about all the extra cruft that apps leave behind? AppZapper handled it. 

This week, the app returned from a long hiatus to introduce a brand-new version of “the uninstaller Apple forgot” with AppZapper 3000.

Uninstalling apps has never been so satisfying

The timing is pretty good. Remember Launchpad? It featured the most user-friendly method for uninstalling software, at least for installations from the Mac App Store. You could hold the Option key to reveal an X icon that uninstalled the app from your Mac.

But Launchpad went away with macOS 26 Tahoe, and it’s not one of the decisions that Apple revisited with macOS 27 Golden Gate. Launchpad was only ever able to “uninstall” software from the App Store though, and that was never as thorough as AppZapper.

Anyway, AppZapper 3000 replaces a very legacy version of the app (that still worked!) while adding some really fun and interactive features.

Part of the AppZapper appeal has always been the signature sound effect that accompanies each zap. Now zapping isn’t just a sonic experience. Check it out:

AppZapper 3000 includes three “zaps” before requiring a license, and it’s just as satisfying as ever to use. Your cursor literally turns into a blaster, allowing you to aim and eliminate each bit of app cruft, like a video game.

You can try AppZapper 3000 for free here, and a license costs just $18.

title: Why watchOS 27 removes the useful multitasking feature on Apple Watch
snippet: watchOS 27 removes a useful multitasking shortcut from Apple Watch. While we don’t know if it will make a return, we at least now know why the gesture was removed. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 removes a useful multitasking shortcut from Apple Watch. While we don’t know if it will make a return, we at least now know why the gesture was removed.

Live Rewind replaces switching between apps, but only on Series 12 and Ultra 4

Prior to updating to watchOS 27, Apple Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, and SE 3 support a shortcut for jumping between apps.

You can double-click the Digital Crown to instantly switch between the current app and the previously used app. It also works for jumping between the watch face and the last viewed app.

It’s great for quickly switching contexts with just muscle memory and not tapping the display.

But, as we’ve flagged a few times, the double-click gesture is gone from watchOS 27. 

The reason in part is a hardware-specific feature that’s coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 later this year.

Apple announced last week that Live Rewind, a feature that provides a 15-second transcript of spoken audio, is coming to the new watches. It’s part of the Audio Intelligence feature set that includes Siri Recap as well.

The way to invoke Live Rewind is by double-clicking the Digital Crown.

Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3, and earlier Apple Watches will not support Live Rewind

That explains why the gesture was freed up for watchOS 27. However, it’s not an especially satisfying explanation for a few reasons.

First, what about Apple Watches without Live Rewind? The gesture just opens the new dynamic app grid — same as a single click.

	

Second, not everyone will want to use the Live Rewind feature. That’s fine. You can control when and how Audio Intelligence features are used. However, we shouldn’t expect Apple to give us back the missing gesture.

At any rate, it seems like an opportunity for a nice settings option. Maybe watchOS 27.1 or 27.2 can do something with the feedback.

For now, it’s a bit of an awkward situation with the feature not shipping yet and only on new hardware. The answer may just be to trust the dynamic app grid, hoping that one of the five suggested apps around Siri includes what you need.

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

title: Apple Watch adds an all-new Readiness app, here’s how it works
snippet: Apple Watch is gaining an all-new health-related app called Readiness. Here’s what you need to know about Apple’s new fitness-focused Readiness app. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch is gaining an all-new health-related app called Readiness. Here’s what you need to know about Apple’s new fitness-focused Readiness app.

Readiness app for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

Apple’s new Readiness app is part of the upgraded Health Sensing System on Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. 

“Redesigned with more capable optical and electrical sensors and larger, more power-efficient green LEDs, the sensing system unlocks deeper health and fitness insights,” Apple says.

The new hardware helps inform Apple’s new Readiness app. For that reason, you’ll need to upgrade to a Series 12 or Ultra 4 to experience the new Apple Watch app.

The new watches are available to pre-order now ahead of release on Friday.

Before the Readiness app actually arrives, you can see it in action in a few places.

First, the App Store listing is already live. This is to support redownloading the pre-installed app on Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches in case the app is deleted. 

However, you still need a new Apple Watch to unlock the app. It’s not included on Apple Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, or SE 3 and earlier, even with watchOS 27.

This is from the App Store description:

Get a score and a clear classification of your readiness, including Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It.

See an explanation of relevant factors and tap through to associated apps.

Add complications and Smart Stack widgets for convenient and glanceable insights.

View additional details in the Fitness app on

You can also see the new Readiness app shown off in Apple’s Series 12 introduction video:

As for how the new Readiness app actually works, Apple has a new support document that explains everything you need to know. 

As mentioned during the keynote, Readiness is based on a score of 0-10:

Go for it: 8–10

Ready: 5–7

Pace Yourself: 2–4

Recover: 0–1

Apple also explains how “Activity data, daytime and overnight vitals, and sleep data” all impact your Readiness score:

Activity: Activity from both today and your recent history can impact your readiness score. Active calories, workout effort ratings, and Training Load data are all used to calculate the score. Increased activity in general can reduce your score, while steady or reduced activity raises it. Additionally, you might see your score go down during the day after a workout or activity.

Vitals: Readiness considers the status of your daytime and overnight metrics from the Vitals app. When your vitals indicate you’re Notably or Slightly off, your score is reduced. When all of your metrics are Typical or Favorable, your score is raised. Higher-than-usual heart rate variability (HRV) can lead to Favorable vitals and a high readiness score.

Sleep: Your sleep score from the previous night and your recent history can impact your readiness score. A low sleep score from poor-quality or inconsistent sleep can reduce your readiness score, while a high sleep score, or an improved sleep score, can raise your readiness score.

Sleep score has been a really helpful built-in feature, and readiness score will take it even further with new hardware.

9to5Mac’s Take

It’s great to see Apple Watch introduce Readiness as a built-in app as part of the new Health Sensing System.

While it would be nice to have it on watches without upgrading, it’s understandable that the new system relies on the vastly upgraded heart rate monitor.

For folks not upgrading hardware, there are already ways to use health and fitness data to come up with a similar system as well.

Meanwhile, Apple is treating its latest hardware as a clear shot at the competition by just becoming a better Apple Watch in ways that count.

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

Apple TV has one of its best shows, Slow Horses, returning tonight for season 6 (watch here). And the streamer has just announced that seasons 7 and 8 are both already in the works.

Slow Horses gets season 8 renewal ahead of tonight’s season 6 premiere

Most shows in the streaming TV era have too long of waits between seasons. But Apple TV hit Slow Horses is a stark exception.

Slow Horses first premiered in 2022, and now just a few years later, its sixth season kicks off tonight.

You can watch Slow Horses season 6 here once it becomes available tonight at 9 p.m. ET.

The short, six-episode length of each season likely helps the show stay so prolific. But so too does Apple renewing it for new seasons far in advance.

That’s what just happened again. Joining the previously announced season 7, Apple just confirmed that season 8 is coming too.

Season 8 will be adapted from “Clown Town,” the ninth novel in Mick Herron’s “Slough House” book series. It’s also the final novel in the series—for now. Here’s the official summary:

Season eight sees Jackson Lamb and Diana Taverner face off in their most explosive confrontation yet. When a botched attempt to blackmail the Park puts Taverner on the offensive, it is up to Lamb to unravel one of MI5’s darkest secrets and put an end to it once and for all.

Based on Apple’s typical release schedule, we’ll likely see season 7 premiere in 2027 and season 8 in 2028. Here’s hoping Herron will publish a new book in the meantime so that work can begin on Slow Horses season 9.

title: Instagram chief thinks a chronological feed is ‘much worse’ and says the quiet part out loud
snippet: As new legislation in Australia aims to let users opt out of the algorithmic nature of modern social media, Instagram’s Adam Mosseri has said that the experience of a chronological feed is “much worse.” more…
fullText:
As new legislation in Australia aims to let users opt out of the algorithmic nature of modern social media, Instagram’s Adam Mosseri has said that the experience of a chronological feed is “much worse.”

Reported by ABC, Mosseri said that “the average user experience gets much worse” when going back to a chronological feed. The Instagram chief added:

If you go to a chronological feed, it ends up getting overwhelmed with content from companies, brands, and publishers… Creators get drowned out, and then your friends get drowned out even more… You miss a lot more content … and you spend a lot less time on the platform…

That last bit is pretty telling, but there’s certainly a point to be made here.

In a chronological feed versus an algorithmic one, a larger quantity of posts would indeed improve reach and, as such, constantly-online influencers, businesses, and others would absolutely benefit from their ability to post more content. That could drown out content from close friends, assuming the user is actually following all of these other accounts in the first place. 

	

Mosseri says that engagement dropped by as much as 50% when switching back to a chronological feed. While Australia is looking to give users an opt-out from algorithmic feeds, Instagram has already complied with legislation that requires it to give the choice to the user such as in the Netherlands, the report brings out. All users can switch to a chronological feed today, but the app always defaults to the algorithmic feed when it is opened.
