title: Apple on wide Android foldables beating iPhone Duo; ‘they got the aspect ratio’
snippet: If it feels like it’s been a quiet week for Android news, it’s not just because Monday was a holiday in the US. As is often the case, pretty much everyone got out of the way of Apple’s latest iPhone announcement, which saw the company launch its first-ever foldable. Joining the party this late is down to lead to some questions towards the company’s leadership, but a new interview with Apple’s fresh-faced CEO helps shine some light on how the brand views its Duo competitors. more…
fullText:
If it feels like it’s been a quiet week for Android news, it’s not just because Monday was a holiday in the US. As is often the case, pretty much everyone got out of the way of Apple’s latest iPhone announcement, which saw the company launch its first-ever foldable. Joining the party this late is down to lead to some questions towards the company’s leadership, but a new interview with Apple’s fresh-faced CEO helps shine some light on how the brand views its Duo competitors.

The folks at Tom’s Guide and TechRadar sat down with Apple CEO John Ternus and SVP of Marketing Greg Joswiak to dish on the iPhone Duo, and the pair had some thoughts for their Android-based competition. Ternus started with a comment on what he sees as “cheap-feeling plastic” surfaces on devices like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold or Galaxy Z Fold 8, praising the Duo’s nanotexture finish as the solution to the typical polymer displays foldables are required to use. Ternus also pointed out that the device was largely kept secret, though that “they” — Samsung and other rivals, presumably — managed to learn about the aspect ratio ahead of time.

Ternus and Joz also commented on the software side of the device, pointing to their relationships with developers as a reason the iPhone Duo will outperform its competitors when the device launches next month. The pair specifically highlighted Slack, Netflix, and Zoom as apps that will be optimized for the foldable come day one, though early adopters should definitely prep themselves for some familiar black borders. Apparently, the month and a half gap between the Duo’s announcement and its launch date is also part of the plan, echoing back to the three-month gap the iPad received in 2010 to give third-parties time to make changes to their apps.

Apple also sees the redesigned iOS experience on the Duo as the smartest way to approach foldable software, calling it “incredibly intuitive” and helping to make the overall experience “continuous. I will say, paired with some truly slick animations when opening the display, Apple’s foldable iPhone could have a leg up on its Android competition in that regard, and I’m fascinated to see how companies like Samsung and Google respond to a company as traditionally conservative in its design doing something as massive as moving the dock. Those answers, I would think, will likely arrive throughout 2027.

	

The entire interview, embedded above, is worth a watch, even if I assume most of the people reading this article likely aren’t interested in switching to the iPhone Duo. Ternus and Joz also tackle the stylus question — in their eyes, Jobs’ famous quote about using a stylus with a smartphone doesn’t apply here — and claim they see the Duo as “a great value.” Plus, it’s a chance to get better acquainted with Apple’s new CEO outside of following orders in renaming Lake Ontario in Apple Maps, just as the Sundar Pichai-led Google did last month.

title: Xbox’s clever disc-to-digital feature was 15 years in the making
snippet: When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox's ongoing game preservation efforts. Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft's plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, rec … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox’s ongoing game preservation efforts.

Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, recycling digital games, and the ability to swap discs at retail stores in exchange for a digital version. Some of those original Xbox One plans leaked out online, and many others have remained secret for more than a decade.

Microsoft’s Xbox One launch hinted at some of these ideas, too. The console was originally supposed to be always online, to enable Microsoft’s vision of digital game sharing, and more. Microsoft walked back those plans after a messy and confusing Xbox One launch created a backlash to the always-online requirement. But some of those original digital ideas are now starting to come to life in different ways.

Microsoft’s decision to essentially embed a serial number on the discs that Xbox consoles can read has allowed it to launch disc-to-digital, a method that lets you turn a physical Xbox One disc into a digital copy simply by slotting it into a disc drive. A decision made 15 years ago has resulted in this useful feature and may well lead to true digital ownership in the coming years.

It’s not something Sony can copy, either. Unless the PlayStation maker has been quietly adding metadata to its discs over the years, it will have to find another method to help PS5 owners move their physical collections over to the digital era.

Microsoft thought ahead, not necessarily to disc-to-digital, but just about identifying discs so it was ready for when console games moved into an all-digital era. That era looks like it’s right around the corner, especially now that Sony has announced it’s killing PlayStation discs in 2028. Both Microsoft and Sony also ship digital-only variants of their consoles, and it’s clear from game sales numbers that most titles are purchased digitally these days.

I fully expect Microsoft to follow Sony and eventually scrap Xbox discs, especially as the number of authorized manufacturers capable of producing physical media continues to shrink. That’s largely because almost every other form of media, from music to movies, has moved on from optical discs. The big difference with Xbox, though, is that Microsoft has always been obsessed with game preservation.

In the same year that disc-to-digital is launching, Microsoft is also bringing original Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC. The company has also spent years working on its backward compatibility program, to get as many games from the Xbox and Xbox 360 eras working on modern Xbox consoles. Game preservation is a central part of Project Helix, the next Xbox that could play every Xbox game ever made.

It’s not an easy task to pull off game preservation, either. There are the complex technical challenges that need to be overcome, alongside licensing issues and the business challenges from publishers that decide how a game should be sold.

Some of those technical challenges mean that not every single Xbox One disc will work with this new disc-to-digital feature. That could be because some early discs simply didn’t get pressed with the unique identifier. Microsoft warned its internal Xbox testers that “it all depends on how and when the disc was manufactured and it may not have the features we need for this program.”

Discs that are slightly damaged might also not work with disc-to-digital, but run just fine otherwise. That’s why it’s important that Xbox is launching this right now — physical media decays over time.

The licensing and business challenges are far more complicated. Publishers need to agree to disc-to-digital, and some could hold back. It appears that most are on board, and even Ubisoft games started showing up recently. We’ve seen a number of other games come online since Microsoft’s announcement, and the company has been clear that more will follow.

The next challenge beyond disc-to-digital is solving digital ownership. If all we really own of a digital game is a license, I hope that one day those licenses can move freely across devices and platforms. I want to buy a single copy of a game and have that license follow me across Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, and PC. I also want to be able to gift or sell that license on different marketplaces, just as we’ve been able to do with physical discs at retailers for decades.

Microsoft envisioned this true digital ownership future 15 years ago, and it has gradually taken steps toward making it a reality. I hope Xbox can eventually pull it off, but the solution will require publishers and platform owners to agree on a shared system for how game licenses are bought, transferred, gifted, and resold. That’s a much bigger challenge than simply getting rid of the disc.

The pad

Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th. Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month, and I’ll be there too. More than two years since the last major Windows event, Microsoft is holding a Windows and Surface event that will include a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be in attendance, alongside Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. The surprise guest? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. I wouldn’t be surprised if this event is mainly focused on RTX Spark PCs, and don’t be surprised to hear more about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra pricing and availability.

The Gates Foundation says it’s spending $1 billion to expand access to AI. Over the next two years, the Gates Foundation plans to spend at least $1 billion on improving access to AI in education, healthcare, and agriculture. The funds will go toward creating AI datasets in more languages and making AI access more affordable.

Microsoft says ‘people matter more than AI’ following safety concerns. Microsoft published a 37-page AI code of conduct this week, in the midst of researchers warning that AI progress could outpace human control. Microsoft’s AI code of conduct makes it clear that “people matter more than AI,” and that AI models are not conscious and “should not be designed to imitate consciousness.” That’s a direct swipe at Anthropic, which has been pushing the idea of AI welfare and model consciousness lately. The code of conduct also commits to ensuring Microsoft’s own models will remain under human control and discourage “patterns of interaction that cause excessive reliance or emotional dependence.”

Microsoft adds Grok to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Microsoft added SpaceXAI’s Grok models to its Foundry service last year, and now it’s expanding access to Copilot itself. Grok models can now be used in Word, Excel and PowerPoint from the model picker interface for Microsoft Frontier users. Microsoft says it’s starting with a preview release to “gather feedback.” This means Office Copilot users can now pick between OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude models, and SpaceXAI’s Grok models.

Microsoft issues emergency Windows 11 update to fix its record-breaking patch. Last week I reported on Microsoft’s record-breaking patch Tuesday, and it turns out that this giant set of fixes has caused some issues. Microsoft has had to release an out-of-band patch to fix folder shares on Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines, Remote Desktop Services sessions, and some USB audio devices. These out-of-band updates used to be a rare occurrence, but there have already been eight this year alone. With AI models continuing to spot even more vulnerabilities in Windows, I can’t see this all slowing down anytime soon. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if October’s patch Tuesday breaks another record.

BlizzCon delivers the return of StarCraft, Diablo on Netflix, and Diablo V. StarCraft is returning in 2030, after more than decade of lying dormant. The new title, announced onstage at BlizzCon last weekend, will be an open-world shooter instead of a top-down real-time strategy game. Blizzard is also working on a new animated series of Diablo with Netflix, and teased that Diablo V is coming in spring 2029.

Microsoft is finally adding a setting for remapping the Copilot key. If you picked up an Arm-powered Copilot Plus PC over the past years, you may have noticed the new Copilot key that launches Microsoft’s digital assistant. The latest Release Preview builds of Windows 11 add a setting to change the AI key back to a control or context menu button, so you don’t accidentally hit it and launch Copilot.

Microsoft’s head of comms is leaving after almost 20 years. Frank Shaw, chief communications officer at Microsoft, is leaving the company at the end of the year. Shaw has been at the heart of Microsoft’s communications for 29 years — nearly 20 years as a Microsoft employee plus time at an external agency before that. He’s well-respected across the public relations industry, and has earned a reputation both inside and outside Microsoft as someone who is direct but respectful. Many employees have told me over the years that they always fear an email from him for misspeaking or accidentally leaking product plans. Microsoft hasn’t appointed a replacement yet, but it sounds like a successor will be named in the coming weeks.

Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it. Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima. While PlayStation framed the swap as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” Kojima revealed it was actually due to an unexpected cancellation notice for Physint in June. The swap now means Xbox is publishing the studio’s next game, OD, as well as Physint. It’ll be interesting to see what exclusivity decisions are made here.

Xbox is bringing back startup animations from its console history. Microsoft has started testing a new Xbox console feature that lets you enable the original Xbox One or Xbox One X boot screens on an Xbox Series S or X console. The update also includes a new search feature, improved Remote Play quality, and clearer voice chat. It’s great to see Xbox continue on its regular monthly console updates.

Microsoft has new AI privacy rules for schools. Microsoft agreed to a set of safety and privacy principles for AI in schools a week after two major school systems announced a ban on student-facing AI. The agreement with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the second-largest teachers union in the US, sees Microsoft commit to 10 principles that can be contractually enforced. This includes limits on the amount of data Microsoft collects from students or educators and a pledge not to train AI models on this data. New York City and Los Angeles have both implemented one-year bans on AI tools for lots of students, giving the districts more time to consider guardrails.

Microsoft’s Windows chief wants to remake Windows for both human and agent users. Pavan Davuluri, head of Windows and devices at Microsoft, caused some controversy when he tweeted last year that Windows was an agentic OS. That made many think Microsoft was abandoning Windows users in favor of AI, but Davuluri is now making things a lot clearer in an interview with GeekWire’s Mary Jo Foley. “The user of Windows going forward will continue to be users … but it’s also going to add these agentic workloads,” said Davuluri. “There is no one single sort of ring for a billion-plus users on the platform.”

Blizzard workers secure a major union contract. The nearly 1,900 workers across Blizzard have secured a contract with Microsoft that include “really strong” layoff protections. The World of Warcraft unit had to fight for a contract, and the teams that work on Overwatch, Diablo, quality assurance, and more helped put the pressure on to extend the union contract to all Blizzard employees. It comes just two months after Xbox announced significant layoffs that will impact 3,200 employees over the course of the current financial year.

The woman fixing a Microsoft mess with brutal honesty. The Wall Street Journal has published a profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. It’s mostly a recap of Sharma’s career and how she got the top Xbox job, but it also includes some funny anecdotes. Surprisingly, Sharma spends a few hours each month personally responding to Xbox customer support tickets to better understand players. Since becoming Xbox CEO, she’s also received wedding invitations in the mail, presumably from the same fans that paste her face on images of Jesus Christ.

title: Finally, You Can Paint Your Kitchen to Match Your Slow Cooker
snippet: Crock-Pot and Valspar are the duo we didn’t know we needed.
fullText:
As someone who is slowly but surely color-drenching my entire home, I’m not ashamed to admit that, yes, I would design an entire kitchen around a single stylish appliance. I know I’m not alone. And what could boost my home’s aesthetic more than a kitchen that matches the slow cooker?

Crock-Pot, the renowned slow cooker brand, has teamed up with Valspar to release six new slow-cooker colors, each with matching paint swatches. So if you’re looking to give your kitchen a makeover this fall, one of these color pairings may inspire your next design move.

The launch comes just ahead of fall, peak slow cooker season, at a time when color-drenching and using chic appliances as a focal point continue to be popular interior design trends.

“We wanted to reimagine what a slow cooker can look like in today’s kitchen — not only a hardworking appliance, but a beautifully designed piece that feels at home on the countertop,” Mallory Fuller-Guzman, a senior manager at Newell Brands, said in a statement regarding the launch. The new Crock-Pots are also meant to inspire people “to create spaces that feel personal and reflective of the way they live.”

Will somebody repaint their entire kitchen to match one of the new Crock-Pot colors? We’ll probably find out if we scroll Instagram long enough.

	

			

The new Crock-Pot colors

title: I tried Tovala’s smart oven for two weeks — here’s whether it beats takeout
snippet: Tovala offers both a smart oven and a meal-delivery service. Its meals come with QR codes that you scan using the app, allowing the oven to automatically follow the cooking instructions.
fullText:
I tried Tovala’s smart oven for two weeks to see if it could actually make dinner as easy as the company promises. It won’t replace the quality of a good home-cooked meal, and some dishes turned out better than others, but it’s hard to beat the convenience on days when you absolutely don’t want to cook.

This was exactly the challenge that Tovala co-founder and CEO David Rabie aimed to address. 

“The idea originated from my own struggles in business school. I was often busy and sought a solution as convenient as takeout or frozen meals, yet still wanted the experience of a genuine home-cooked dish,” Rabie told TechCrunch via email. 

“One afternoon, I was making a meal using several different appliances and realized that I was mostly just pressing buttons,” he said. “That’s what led to the idea for an end-to-end system: fresh, mostly prepped meals paired with a connected oven that could cook them automatically. The challenge became figuring out how to remove all that friction without sacrificing the experience of eating food that was actually cooked fresh at home.”

The idea is pretty simple: Tovala sends you meals with the ingredients already portioned out, and its smart oven handles the cooking.

Instead of chopping vegetables, measuring ingredients, figuring out cooking temperatures, and standing over a stove, you mostly just unwrap everything, follow simple instructions like adding packets of seasoning, put everything in the provided trays, scan a QR code using the companion app, and let the oven do the rest. 

The countertop-sized oven follows the cooking instructions automatically, switching temperatures and cooking modes throughout the process. It can bake, broil, air fry, toast, and reheat. The regular oven costs $299, while the Smart Oven Pro costs $349 and adds a steam function.

Image Credits:Tovala

As for the meal-delivery side, there are more than 45 meals to choose from each week. For instance, steak and garlic mashed potatoes, salmon with vegetables, butternut squash soup, pasta dishes, and more. 

There are also plenty of options when it comes to how much food you want delivered. Meal plans include 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, or 16 meals per week. You can skip deliveries, pause your plan, or cancel if you don’t need meals that week. 

The meals aren’t exactly cheap, though. Single-serving meals start at $13.99, and two-serving meals start at around $8.99 per serving — $17.98 total — plus a $10.99 shipping fee. The company also recently launched family-sized meals, starting at $35.96. Unlike meal-delivery rivals like HelloFresh, Tovala is essentially betting that you’re willing to pay for the added convenience of having most of the cooking handled for you. 

Taste and quality were the parts I was most skeptical about going in. I’m not a professional chef by any means, but I’ve recently gotten much more interested in cooking. Once you start learning how to properly sear meat, roast vegetables, and build flavor yourself, it’s hard not to be suspicious of a machine that promises to do all of that for you.

The biggest downside for me was the texture of the meats and how they cooked in the oven. I like a steak with a nice crust, so I finished mine in a steel pan for some extra browning. The steak was much better afterward, but that obviously defeats the point of a process that’s supposed to be mostly hands-off.

Not every dish had that problem, though. One of my favorites was the pineapple shrimp stir-fry. The rice was well cooked, and the sauce had plenty of flavor. It wasn’t necessarily something I’d rave about compared with a great restaurant meal, but it was easy, satisfying, and required very little effort.

Image Credits:Tovala

What I  appreciated most, however, was the grocery-food feature that gives the oven some use beyond cooking Tovala-branded meals. The oven can recognize certain grocery-store products, so instead of guessing how long your frozen waffles need to toast, you can scan the barcode and let the oven automatically select the appropriate settings.

That’s what makes Tovala feel more like a genuinely smart oven, not just a machine built to cook its own meal kits. Even if you stop ordering Tovala meals, you can still use the oven with compatible grocery products.

Overall, if your alternative to cooking is ordering takeout because you’re too tired to cook, Tovala makes a pretty compelling case for itself.

Tovala is available on the company’s website and Amazon. It ships to most U.S. states, but it doesn’t currently ship to Alaska or Hawaii.

title: Another Miserably Hot Summer Is Nearly Over. NOAA Says It’s the Worst on Record
snippet: The heat was immense, and that’s bad news for already rising utility bills.
fullText:
If you sat around at any point this year and wondered why it felt so much hotter than normal, it’s because it actually was. According to a new report from NOAA, summer 2026 is the hottest on record, beating out the prior holders of the crown, a tie between 2021 and 1936. 

Per NOAA, the average temperature across the continental US was 75.6 degrees Fahrenheit, with daytime maximum temperatures averaging out at 88.6 degrees. Both of those are the warmest since the beginning of recorded temperatures in the US. Most of this extra heat was concentrated in the southern and western portions of the US, while the Midwest, Great Lakes region and northeastern areas all saw near or slightly above average temperatures. 

Some areas have it worse than others. Arizona had its second-hottest summer on record, trailing only 2024. However, the desert state still experienced an average of 97 degrees, with 39 days with temperatures over 110 degrees and 121 days over 100 degrees. The state is expected to add to those totals heading into the last couple of weeks of September. 

Alaska and Hawaii weren’t left out of the party. Both of those states experienced their third-warmest summers on record.

To add insult to injury, nearly 60% of the country is also in drought conditions, according to the US Drought Monitor. NOAA says that the Ohio Valley and parts of the Midwest had good rain but virtually everywhere else received less rain than average. Somewhat ironically, two years ago, the script was flipped, and both of those regions were in drought conditions. 

“Persistent heat domes and drought conditions were key factors in the widespread above-average temperatures observed during 2026,” Karin Gleason, chief of the monitoring section at NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information, told CNET in an email. Gleason says that the jet stream, which is the strong wind in Earth’s atmosphere that functionally dictates the weather, was skewed toward high pressure in the US, trapping heat and causing extended heat domes. Pair that with drought conditions, which allowed “solar energy to heat the dry ground and air more efficiently,” and you have the ingredients for one hot summer. 

The unseasonable warmth is going to continue

Hurricane Lowell hit Ni’ihau and Kaua’i. It’s the first hurricane to directly hit Kaua’i since Hurricane Iniki in 1992. NOAA

Summertime heat is often oppressive, but it’s not the only season this year that is slated to have warmer-than-average temperatures. NOAA released another report showing that 2026’s El Niño is strengthening, and is 90% likely to continue doing so into winter 2026 to 27. That means the US — and many other parts of the Northern Hemisphere — are in for an unseasonably warm autumn and winter. 

El Niño is a normal weather pattern caused by warmer-than-average conditions in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean every two to seven years and can last up to 18 months. However, the current one began forming in June and has risen to the rank of “super” El Niño, a media-only name that NOAA doesn’t use, which indicates that this year’s El Niño is reaching historic levels.

It changes weather patterns all across the world, and is to blame for the uptick of hurricane threats in Hawaii, the lack of hurricane threats in the Atlantic, and higher-than-average temperatures for Americans across the country. Experts predict that El Niño is going to last until February 2027 at least, leading to a warmer winter, but also an increased chance of extreme weather, not unlike the winter storm that buried much of the US under up to a foot of snow in January. Warmer doesn’t necessarily mean that it won’t be cold enough for snow.

And you’re paying for all of it

With temperatures reaching record highs, it’s no surprise that utility bills likely did too. Analysts warned that electricity demand could spike over the summer of 2026. Those increases definitely happened, as the US Energy Information Administration showed that fossil fuel prices were up virtually all summer, with the one hopeful stat being that solar, wind and hydroelectric power generation were up while fossil fuel usage was down compared to 2025. 

Data about the actual impact to consumer bills isn’t out yet, but early estimates show that the nationwide average bill went up by 4%, with some areas reaching as high as 10%, including Detroit, Baltimore, and Washington DC. A few major cities saw a decline, but most places saw some sort of increase. 

Read more: Our Exclusive Lab Tests Reveal Whether Portable or Window AC Units Work Better to Keep You Cool

Most of these costs aren’t coming from an increase in usage from everyday people in their homes. According to the EIA, homes used 1,500 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2025, which is up a small amount from the 1,400 TWh that residents used in 2005. That means people are using less than 10% more power today than they were back when Hollaback Girl by Gwen Stefani ruled FM radio stations.

By contrast, data centers used approximately 70 TWh in 2015. They more than doubled that number to 176 TWh in 2023 and are up to 448 TWh in 2025, with expectations that the number is going to increase to 980 TWh by 2030. That means data center energy usage went up by 272 TWh in just three years, versus 100 TWh in residential homes over 20 years. The amount of power used by data centers in 2026 is still unknown, but based on the frequency at which they’re being built, it’s hard to imagine that data center energy usage is going down. 

The human cost is also rising. According to the World Health Organization, heat-related deaths worldwide have increased by 85% between the year 2000 and 2021, and a recent NPR investigation found that the number of deaths influenced by heat in the US is far higher than the official CDC figures. All of those data sources indicate that heat-related deaths are increasing in the face of global climate change, including approximately 35,000 excess deaths from Europe’s back-to-back heat waves during summer 2026.

title: Apple showcases iPhone 18 Pro camera with new ‘What Holds Us’ photography exhibition
snippet: Apple is holding a new photography exhibition in New York City this weekend to showcase the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is holding a new photography exhibition in New York City this weekend to showcase the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Here are the details.

’Images that speak to presence as both a state of mind and a way of being’

If you are in the New York area this weekend, Apple is opening a new photography exhibition featuring original work shot entirely on the iPhone 18 Pro.

Running from September 18 through September 20 at 456 West 18th Street in New York City, Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibition will feature work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity,” the company says.

The exhibition was curated by Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, and is meant to showcase the range of creative possibilities enabled by the iPhone 18 Pro’s new camera system, including its variable aperture.

According to Apple, Chin’s work focuses on the Bugaboo Mountains in British Columbia, where he photographed climbers against the surrounding landscape. His images range from tight close-ups to wide panoramas and action shots.

Here’s Chin:

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. (…) I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Jack Davison went for a more intimate approach, photographing people interacting with clay and chalk inside a former sugar warehouse in London.

Commenting on the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera, he said:

“I genuinely was blown away by the camera on iPhone 18 Pro. (…) There was something about the quality of the imagery that felt like a huge leap. Not just from a technical standpoint, but in its ability to create more artistic and surreal images. That really surprised me. The ability to switch between lenses, use slower shutters, and shoot RAW made it such a potent package.”

As for Alex Prager, she created large-scale crowd scenes on a soundstage in Los Angeles, combining wide overhead shots with tighter portraits and details.

Here’s Prager on what she took away from the experience:

“Photography has changed a lot, and this particular camera is more like a video stream, in essence, which also shapes how we approach images today — more like video with higher output in our photo albums and on social media. (…). It was exciting for me to think about all of this while harking back to a timeless crowd winding down from a celebration.”

title: It took way too long for someone to make USB-C cables that say what they can actually do [Gallery]
snippet: Life with USB-C is great, except for the one nagging problem that’s been there since the beginning – you never really know what you’re getting. While it’s not quite the “Wild West” anymore, I was thrilled to see that someone finally made a collection of USB-C cables that not only do what they say they’ll do, but literally have their specs printed on the cable itself. more…
fullText:
Life with USB-C is great, except for the one nagging problem that’s been there since the beginning – you never really know what you’re getting. While it’s not quite the “Wild West” anymore, I was thrilled to see that someone finally made a collection of USB-C cables that not only do what they say they’ll do, but literally have their specs printed on the cable itself.

USB-C is probably one of the most underrated things to happen in mobile tech, maybe ever? Even 10 years ago it was still hard to imagine being able to use the same cable type across your phone, tablet, laptop, or anything else, but that’s very much the reality of today. In theory, one could go on a trip with just a single USB-C cable and be able to charge up their laptop, smartphone, tablet, gaming handheld, headphones, and a number of other pieces of tech with just that one cable. There are still dedicated cables for some things, like smartwatches, but the “Universal” part of USB finally feels true.

The problem is just that it’s really hard to buy the right cable.

It’s not hard to find a USB-C cable – they’re literally everywhere. But the one problem with this standard is that it’s so flexible that two different cables can serve wildly different tasks. A basic cable might be able to charge up a phone at around 20W, but not be able to transfer data at all.. Meanwhile, another cable on the higher end might support 12x the power while also being capable of display output and 40GBps of data transfer. Yet, at a glance, they probably look essentially identical. Even if you bought the right cable for a specific application – let’s say charging a laptop at 100W – you might not be able to tell it apart from the dozen others in your bag.

	

I’ve been frustrated by this problem countless times over the years, and equally annoyed that there wasn’t a good solution to finding the “right” cable besides just ordering a new one. So I’m glad to see that someone has finally fixed this – though I’d never have guessed it’d be a YouTube channel’s merch shop.

LTTStore launched “TrueSpec” cables early this year with the promise of not only strictly adhering to USB-C spec on the cables it sells, but also clearly messaging what the cable can do on both the packaging and the cable itself. It took way too long for someone to do this consistently. There have been cables here or there with labels, but it’s been rare and usually with some negative factor, like inconsistent labeling or a small lineup.

“TrueSpec” hits what I’ve wanted. Each cable has a label etched into either end, quickly identifying what power and data transfer speeds the cable is capable of. The cables themselves aren’t anything fancy beyond this label, but the build quality is obvious with some thick rubber sheathing. Admittedly, I do wish the cable was thinner – it’s pretty bulky and heavy, which is a little annoying in a backpack – but the pros outweigh the cons in my book. 

They’re also admittedly not cheap at all. USB C-C cables start at around $22 and A-C at around $17. 

LTT TrueSpec USB C-C cables

LTT TrueSpec USB A-C cables

	

It’s not like this is some completely unprecedented idea. 

Labels on USB-C cables have been done before, and there are options out there with labels on the cable ends just like this – the organization behind USB-C even has documentation on how to implement this for crying out loud. It’s just so uncommon that “TrueSpec” is easily the most polished and clear effort to actually deliver on this idea. 

LTTStore also sent out some of their other products – this article isn’t sponsored in any way, to be clear – including the infamous LTT Screwdriver and Precision Kit, and I’ve enjoyed using them both. The Screwdriver in, well, screwdriver tasks, and the Precision Kit has been a great add-on to my recent endeavor to clean out my closet of old “spicy pillow” smartphone batteries by removing those batteries from the phone for easier disposal – more on that in a coming 9to5Google Weekender edition.

Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram

fullText:
A Mac desk setup usually starts with the computer, maybe a display, and a few favorite accessories. But the chair deserves a place on that upgrade list, too. It’s what supports you. Whether you spend your day writing, editing photos, or moving between meetings, it’s something you use in every part of the workday.

The Sihoo B300 Pro puts adjustability at the center of that setup. It combines 4D MicroFit Lumbar Support, 6D All-around Armrests, backrest and seat depth adjustments, an intelligent recline system, and breathable mesh. Together, those features give you more ways to tailor the chair to your body and the way you work.

Fine-tune your lumbar support

Start with the lumbar support. Your back will thank you. Sihoo’s 4D MicroFit system lets you adjust its height and depth, with movement designed to follow your back as you shift position. That gives you control over where the support sits, whether you’re upright at your keyboard or leaning back between tasks.

The idea is to make the fit personal. Two people can use the same desk and display while needing different support from the chair underneath them. Adjustable lumbar support gives you another setting to dial in when putting together your workspace.

Adjust the armrests to match your workflow

The B300 Pro’s 6D All-around Armrests bring that same flexibility to your arms. They rotate, adjust, and flip up, giving you options as you move between desk work and a more relaxed position. You can also move them out of the way when you want more room.

Think about how often your hands change position throughout the day. You might start with a keyboard and trackpad, switch to an iPad for reviewing notes, then pick up your iPhone for a call. Adjustable armrests let you change the chair’s configuration alongside those different activities.

Customize the backrest and seat depth

Backrest and seat depth adjustments add another layer of customization. The backrest offers 2.2 inches of height adjustment, while the seat depth ranges from 16.5 to 18.5 inches. Those separate controls let you fine-tune more than the distance between your seat and the floor.

For a home office, that flexibility can be especially appealing when choosing a chair for an existing desk. You’ve already picked your work surface and arranged your screen. The B300 Pro gives you several ways to work on the fit of your seating, too.

Lean back with intelligent recline

When it’s time to lean back, the intelligent recline system uses a weight-adaptive mechanism to adjust resistance automatically. Sihoo also includes three lockable recline angles: 105, 120, and 135 degrees. You can choose a position for working at your desk or taking a break.

That makes reclining part of the chair’s everyday controls. A workday can include focused typing, reading a long document, and stepping back to think through a project. Having a few positions available gives you options as the pace changes.

Breathable mesh for everyday use

title: iOS 27 gives Apple Photos a very useful feature I’ve wanted for years
snippet: Apple Photos gets a variety of exciting upgrades in iOS 27, including a new feature that’s long been on my wishlist: the ability to save a video frame as a photo. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos gets a variety of exciting upgrades in iOS 27, including a new feature that’s long been on my wishlist: the ability to save a video frame as a photo.

iOS 27 lets you save video frame as a new photo, and it’s much better than screenshots

Have you ever wanted to turn a precious moment from a video into a photo? Historically, the only way to do that has been a screenshot.

But in iOS 27, a much better solution is here: a new ‘Save Video Frame as Photo’ feature.

Taking a screenshot of a video is easy enough. But it comes with two downsides:

Lower resolution photo

Poorly cropped image

With iOS 27’s new feature, both of these become non-issues.

When watching a video in iOS 27’s Photos app, behind the three-dot icon in the top-right corner is a new menu option: ’Save Video Frame as Photo.’

It’s as simple as it sounds. The frame of the video that’s currently being displayed will be saved as a new photo to your Photos library.

The resolution will be far better than what a screenshot offers, and you won’t have to crop it at all. Instead, your iPhone will do all the work for you.

The iPhone has long supported snapping a still frame while you’re actively recording a video. So the lack of a similar option for saved videos has been a curious omission. 

Thankfully now, with iOS 27, Apple finally lets you capture images from a saved video too.

Has this Photos feature been on your personal wishlist too? Let us know in the comments.

title: iOS 27 gives Apple’s Calendar app new feature I’ve wanted for years
snippet: iOS 27 is here, and it adds a new Apple Calendar feature I’ve wanted for years: natural language support when creating events. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is here, and it adds a new Apple Calendar feature I’ve wanted for years: natural language support when creating events.

Natural language now supported for Apple Calendar event creation in iOS 27

I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, but there’s one feature that’s been at the top of my wishlist for as long as I can remember: natural language support.

The excellent third-party app Fantastical has had a robust natural language feature for years. 

Fantastical lets you type all the details about a new event in a single line, just the way you might talk. The app then imports key info like time, location, and invitees without you needing to manually add those separately.

Now with iOS 27, Apple’s Calendar app has finally added a similar feature.

Here are the details per Apple’s website:

Describe an event, add to Calendar. Add and edit events on your calendar with just a description. Easily edit the description to change a lunch meeting to a coffee chat and the Calendar app adjusts the details.

I’ve been using the new feature all summer in the iOS 27 beta, and it’s worked great for me.

If you type in “Work meeting at 3pm,” the event will automatically change the event time to 3. And for other parameters that you may or may not want to add, you’ll see suggestions appear at the top of the keyboard. 

So if you write, “Coffee with Mark at Starbucks,” you can tap the suggestion to add the invitee and/or location to your event, or keep them in the event title instead.

A nice bonus: since the Calendar app also lets you create new reminders, the natural language system extends to any reminders you make.

How much does natural language input matter to you in your calendar app? Let us know in the comments.

title: HBO boss reacts to Apple TV winning more Emmy awards
snippet: Apple TV won big at the Emmys last night, taking home more awards than any other competitor, including HBO. Here’s what HBO boss Casey Bloys said in response to Apple’s victory. more…
fullText:
Apple TV won big at the Emmys last night, taking home more awards than any other competitor, including HBO. Here’s what HBO boss Casey Bloys said in response to Apple’s victory.

HBO head praises Apple TV but says going against trillion-dollar company is ‘a little scary’

Apple TV has long been compared to HBO, with both services prioritizing quality over quantity. Apple has even been called “the new HBO” at times.

Last night’s Emmy awards helped add more support for that claim, with Apple TV beating out HBO, Netflix, and other contenders for the most prizes.

Apple TV became the “most awarded network of the year” with 29 wins overall, including a big night for Widow’s Bay. In second place: HBO with 21 wins.

HBO boss Casey Bloys was asked by Deadline after the awards show for his reaction to Apple’s performance. Here’s what he said:

DEADLINE: What did you think about Apple TV’s performance and their first time finishing as the No. 1 platform at the Emmys?

BLOYS: Well, I’m very happy because I think that they’re very handsome competitors, Zack and Jamie. Look, we’ve had very formidable competitors in going back to Showtime, FX, AMC, Netflix, Amazon, so [when] Apple, everybody, keeps us on our toes, I think we do our best work. It’s a little scary that they’re a trillion-dollar company, but we’ll continue to do what we do, which is put out the best shows that we can.

Bloys has been at HBO since 2004 and became head of all programming in 2016. He’s had a very successful run, and his response to Apple’s win is largely gracious and congratulatory.

However, the most interesting part of the quote is where he says: “It’s a little scary that they’re a trillion-dollar company.”

We don’t know internal budget details for Apple TV specifically. But Apple overall certainly does have more financial leeway than the majority of its competitors—including HBO.

Not so coincidentally, Paramount is trying to buy HBO (and all of Warner Bros. Discovery) in order to better compete with tech giants like Apple and Amazon.

Does Apple’s size automatically give it an edge? Maybe. But as plenty of networks have proven before, money is just one small part of creating beloved content.

title: Motorola’s wide Razr Fold wants to have ‘3D glass’ and a creaseless display
snippet: The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo.

Earlier this month, we obtained internal concept images of what’s very likely the Motorola Razr Fold Wide, though it probably won’t go by that name. They were never published because we didn’t feel there was sufficient supporting evidence at the time. There was no teaser from Motorola at the time, though the images we obtained contained watermarks from Lenovo/Motorola. Those are key to why we’re now posting these.

Motorola’s concept sketches show off a surprising amount of detail. For instance, portions of the mockup are backed by descriptions like “bezel-less” and “3D glass,” referring to the cover display. The latter descriptor sits next to a drawing of a Razr, not the Fold. It still may refer to a new push for a different cover display panel. It’s possible “3D glass” refers to curved screen edges similar to what we often see on the Motorola Edge series.

It also looks like Motorola wants to get closer to Apple’s design philosophy with a bezel-less front display, even with sharp left corners and rounded right edges. Without a bezel, the cover display would have to have the same look as the iPhone Duo. The other option is something like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which uses bezels to soften the harsh corners on the left of the screen.

	

Another page in the document suggests Motorola wants to get as close as possible to a creaseless display with the wide Razr Fold, as seen plainly written across one of the images. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo get extremely close to this, but not quite. Maybe Motorola has the ability to reduce the inner display’s crease to nothing, maybe it’s just marketing talk. Either way, the existing Razr Fold has a more noticeable crease than most, so there’s plenty of room for improvement.

What makes these leaked images worth noting is that the same watermark is used in WPC listings for Motorola Razr devices. It showed up on the existing Razr Fold’s listing back in April, and what brought this to our attention was a new listing posted this week that’s also for the existing Razr Fold, but a Verizon variant of the device. As of now, that doesn’t exist, but the model number is identical outside of a “V” designation that points to a Verizon variant. This updated model also jumps up to the Qi 2.2.1 standard version, though still without magnets inside.

It’s hard to make any definite assessments around the Razr Fold on Verizon based on this listing alone, but the watermark tells us that the leaked materials are almost certainly a real indicator of what Motorola wants to deliver on its wider Razr Fold release.

fullText:
Thomas Ricker

 

is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Pew Research has published a new global survey that sheds light on how people view AI, including its impact on jobs, life in general, and income inequality. The survey questioned 42,151 people across 37 countries from February 8th to May 13th — well ahead of recent apocalyptic warnings.

A majority sees AI as a threat to human employment. In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people are more likely to believe AI will lead to job losses over the next 20 years rather than create new ones. Worries run particularly high in wealthier countries like Australia (76 percent), South Korea (76 percent), and the US (71 percent). Not surprising, given Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s warning that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs.

In general, respondents are more likely to say AI will increase the gap between rich and poor. People from wealthier countries that lean left on the political spectrum tend to believe this the most.

Age also tends to impact viewpoints. Older people are more likely to be more concerned about AI’s impact on daily life than younger people. Younger adults (ages 18–34) are most likely to have mixed feelings about AI and how it will shape the world they’ve inherited. They’re also growing increasingly anxious.

In countries like Sweden, Poland, Japan, Australia, Brazil, and the US, concern among younger demographics has risen sharply over the past year, making them more worried about AI-driven job loss and inequality as older generations in countries like the US and Sweden.

Nevertheless, public sentiment captured by the Pew survey is not wholly negative. Despite economic fears, a global median of 41 percent report feeling equally concerned and excited about AI’s growing presence in daily life, compared to 37 percent who are primarily concerned and just 13 percent who are primarily excited.

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Side Events schedule: NMI, Backblaze, PeakXV Partners, Augment, and more to host
snippet: TechCrunch Disrupt is where the tech community comes together to build, debate, and connect. And while the main event takes over Moscone West from October 13-15, the conversation doesn’t stop when the Expo Hall closes.
fullText:
TechCrunch Disrupt is where the tech community comes together to build, debate, and connect. And while the main event takes over Moscone West from October 13-15, the conversation doesn’t stop when the Expo Hall closes.

The TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Side Event program brings founders, investors, operators, researchers, and tech enthusiasts together across San Francisco for panels, workshops, networking events, parties, and more.

The schedule is growing, with more events being added in the lead-up to Disrupt. Whether you’re looking to meet other founders, connect with investors, dig into a specific technology, or simply spend more time with the tech community, there’s plenty happening around Disrupt.

Check the chronological schedule regularly as new Side Events are added weekly.

Featured Side Events

A few of this year’s Side Events are hosted by TechCrunch partners, bringing the companies and communities behind some of the biggest conversations in tech into the Disrupt Week experience.

Serve, Swipe, & Settle: Mixer for SaaS leaders scaling into embedded payments

October 12 | 5:00 p.m. – 7:00 p.m. PT

Join SaaS founders, developers, and technical leaders at SPIN San Francisco for conversations about turning embedded payments into a revenue stream. Over Ping-Pong, food, and drinks, compare notes on monetization, brand control, and scaling beyond basic payments.

Hosted by: NMI

RSVP↗

The Afterburn: TechCrunch Disrupt Edition

October 14 | 6:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m. PT

Take a break from the pitching, demoing, and networking at this evening mixer. Join founders, builders, investors, and other members of the tech community for cocktails, appetizers, and conversation.

No panels or presentations, just a chance to connect and unwind after a day at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Hosted by: Backblaze and Flamethrower

RSVP↗

Ecosystem Mixer

October 14 | 5:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m. PT

Join Peak XV for a mixer with founders, operators, and investors building what’s next. Good drinks, better conversations, zero pitches required to join our mixer.

Hosted by: PeakXV Partners

RSVP↗

Liquid Assets: A Private Markets Cocktail Party

October 14 | 5:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m. PT

Disrupt is three days of panels. This is not one of them.

Augment and Mintz are hosting a cocktail party Wednesday evening with drinks, light bites, and plenty of room for conversation. No programming or preset meetings, just an opportunity to connect with people across the private markets, technology, and venture ecosystem.

Hosted by: Augment and Mintz

RSVP↗

The Side Event Schedule

Here’s what’s happening around San Francisco during Disrupt week. Events are listed chronologically so you can find something that fits your schedule.

Sunday, October 11

Happy Hour with AI-Created Drinks by AI Barmen

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

Meet AI Barmen, the robotic bartender turning happy hour into an interactive experience. Get personalized drink recommendations and watch as a robotic system prepares and serves your cocktail or mocktail.

Learn more →

EPIC SF Demo Night @ Finding Next Moat

6:00 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

Ten early-stage startups take the stage to make the case for their competitive moat in front of a hand-selected group of venture investors. Stick around after the demos for an open networking session with founders and investors.

Learn more →

International Reception at the European Startup Embassy

6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Join an international startup community for an evening of food, drinks, and networking designed to bring founders, investors, and technology leaders together.

Learn more →

Monday, October 12

The Future of Work Social Mixer + Open Demos: Worktech, Robotics & Agentic AI

5:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Get a preview of the future of work with startup demos, open-mic pitches, and hands-on product showcases spanning work tech, robotics, and agentic AI. Meet founders, operators, and investors exploring how humans and AI will work together.

Learn more →

Open to Work: The Game Show

7:00 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

A live game show and networking night built around the job hunt. Bring your real résumé and compete onstage, and let the audience help decide who advances. The format creates the introductions, so networking happens without the awkward cold approach.

Learn more →

Tuesday, October 13

SF Exclusive VIP Drinks for AI Founders & Accredited Investors

5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.

An invite-only gathering for AI founders and accredited investors following Day 1 of Disrupt. No pitches or panels, just drinks and direct conversations in an intimate setting.

Learn more →

Harvard Griffin GSAS Alumni Networking Mixer

5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.

Connect with Harvard Griffin GSAS alumni during a networking reception for alumni living and working in the Bay Area. Guests are welcome.

Learn more →

South Asian Investor Founder Connect: TechCrunch Disrupt

5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.

Connect with South Asian founders, investors, operators, creators, and technology leaders for an evening of networking and curated introductions across the startup community.

Learn more →

Attacks Never Arrive: Happy Hour

5:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

Join AI founders, security leaders, and operators for an evening of food, drinks, and conversation around social engineering, deepfakes, prompt injection, and the evolving security challenges facing AI.

Learn more →

Content Creators Meetup @ TechCrunch Disrupt

6:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

Founders and creators come together to trade what actually works in founder-led media, from hooks and content strategy to distribution and growth. Expect practical conversation rather than polished keynotes.

Learn more →

Shinhan Square Bridge Meetup @ TechCrunch Disrupt

7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Meet 10 startups from the Shinhan Square Bridge Global program in an intimate evening of conversation, food, and drinks. No pitches or stage programming — just time to connect with founders and explore what’s next.

Learn more →

Wednesday, October 14

NextGen – TechCrunch Disrupt Week 2026

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

The Israel Economic Mission to the West Coast brings together Israeli founders, investors, technology executives, and strategic partners for an invitation-only evening of networking and business conversations.

Learn more →

Love Soul AI Interactive Hologram Superfoods Happy Hour

5:15 p.m. – 7:15 p.m.

Enjoy a superfood-filled happy hour at Salesforce Park featuring Love Soul AI’s interactive hologram, Princess. Stop by after the conference for food, drinks, and a look at the technology in action.

Learn more →

Physical AI After Hours — See the World in 4D

6:00 p.m. – 11:00 p.m.

Explore the future of physical AI, spatial intelligence, robotics, and world models through live 4D capture and reconstruction. Meet founders, researchers, investors, and builders working at the intersection of AI and the physical world.

Learn more →

Hardtech After Party

6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Connect with founders, engineers, investors, and design leaders building the future of hardware, from robotics and wearables to connected devices and medtech. Expect food, drinks, conversation, and a live DJ.

Learn more →

Token Economics: From Cost per Token to Value per Outcome

6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Explore how AI companies turn inference costs into business value, with conversation around model selection, routing, caching, reliability, pricing, and connecting token spend to revenue and customer outcomes.

Learn more →

AI Made Every Candidate Look Perfect. How Do You Find the Real Ones?

6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

When AI can polish every résumé, profile, and interview answer, how do you identify meaningful signal? Join founders, investors, and operators for an intimate conversation about evaluating talent in an AI-first world.

Learn more →

SignalFire’s Disrupt Week Arthaus After-Party

7:00 p.m. – 11:00 p.m.

SignalFire’s annual Disrupt Week after-party returns with live music, immersive art and technology installations, food and drinks, and a gathering of founders, investors, journalists, and builders.

Learn more →

Thursday, October 15

NachoThursday: SaaS & AI Founder + Investor Happy Hour

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

A rooftop happy hour for SaaS and AI founders, C-suite leaders, investors, and tech media. Attendance is limited and guests are screened in advance.

Learn more →

Korea Emerging Tech Showcase

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

Discover emerging technology startups from Korea spanning AI, software, medtech, clean tech, digital platforms, and advanced industrial solutions. The evening features rapid-fire pitches followed by networking with founders, investors, and global partners.

Learn more →

LP, GP & Funded Founder Networking

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

An intimate networking event bringing together LPs, GPs, and funded founders for conversations around technology, venture capital, and the future of the industry.

Learn more →

Fynex x Orion VC | Curated Rooftop Party

6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

A curated rooftop gathering for founders and operators building with AI and investors focused on AI and infrastructure. Expect food, drinks, and an approval-only guest list designed for meaningful conversations.

Learn more →

Side Event Guidelines and Disclaimers

A few things to know before you RSVP:

A Side Event RSVP does not grant access to TechCrunch Disrupt. Side Events are separate from TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, which takes place October 13-15 at Moscone West. You’ll need a valid Disrupt pass or badge to attend the main event.

Side Events are independently operated. Each event is organized and operated solely by its listed host and is not organized, operated, or sponsored by TechCrunch or its affiliates unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Age requirements vary. All Side Events are 18+ unless otherwise specified. Some venues and events may be restricted to guests 21 and older.

Side Events are generally open to the public. Individual hosts may have their own guest lists, capacity limits, approval requirements, or other restrictions, so check the event details before attending.

RSVPs are required where indicated. Please register for each Side Event directly through the RSVP link provided. An RSVP does not guarantee entry if an event reaches capacity or the host has additional admission requirements.

Event details may change. Hosts are responsible for their individual event details, including timing, location, programming, and admission requirements. Check the RSVP page for the latest information before heading out.

More Side Events will be added as we get closer to Disrupt. To see what’s happening and when, the chronological schedule is your friend. It has the full lineup, organized by date and time.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.
